However, it is apparent that the reduction achieved through lower financing costs will not reduce the cost of power for industry to the extent necessary to put the two provinces on a comparable basis with more favoured provinces in our country. Notwithstanding the availability of substantial supplies of coal in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, the situation at the present time is that coal for power in the maritime provinces costs more than coal brought in from the United States for the production of power in Ontario.
While central Canada has, of course, advantages in addition to this one in attracting industry, it has seemed to the government that if the maritime provinces are to be given a fair opportunity to attract industrial growth they must be able to secure coal for the production of power for industrial use at a price that does not exceed the price of United States coal in central Canada. The government has therefore decided that it will provide a subvention on coal used for the production of power in the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia to the extent that is necessary to equalize the cost of that coal with the cost of coal used for the same purposes in Ontario.
I need not emphasize that the subvention on coal will have a double value. It will reduce the cost of the power that is produced from the coal, and that will help greatly. It will also do much to ensure that the coal produced in the maritime provinces continues to be used for the growing power demand of those two provinces and will not be replaced by oil brought in from foreign fields.
This program, I may add, carries the full and enthusiastic support of the premiers of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick and will, I believe, have a lasting and beneficial effect on the economic growth and welfare of the Atlantic region.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO INTRODUCTION OF COMPULSORY INSPECTION
speechtext:
On Friday last the hon. member for Gloucester inquired regarding the possible introduction in 1958 of compulsory inspection of fresh and frozen fish, and as to whether facilities would be made available to those interested in the industry to appear before a committee of the house to discuss any proposed amendments to the regulations enacted under the authority of the Fish Inspection Act.
A decision has not yet been taken regarding amending the regulations enacted under the Fish Inspection Act to provide for the compulsory inspection and grading of fresh and frozen fish. It is not contemplated, however, that a committee of the house will deal with proposed amendments to the regulations. It has been the practice of the department to have full discussion with the industry through its association, the fisheries council of Canada, and with others on proposed amendments to regulations. Meetings with the industry and others interested will be convened before proposals for amending the regulations to provide for compulsory inspection are presented to the government for its consideration.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, November 13, consideration of the motion of Mr. A. R. Smith (Calgary South) for an address to Her Majesty the Queen in reply to her speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Coldwell.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I may say that I was delighted that so much of this sitting was given over to a discussion of the maritime provinces. We are not an overly sensitive people, but we do not like to be ignored. It is a very happy situation for us to find that we are now being considered since this new government has come into office.
Along with the matters that have been discussed heretofore there is in the province of Prince Edward Island another pressing problem which underlies and affects the only three industries of which we may boast, namely agriculture, fishing and the tourist

The Address-Mr. Macquarrie trade. For years and indeed, I think, ever since Prince Edward Island has sent its members to the Canadian parliament there have been discussions about one particular aspect of transportation, namely the link with the mainland. During the administration of Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir Wilfrid Laurier this matter was discussed day in and day out, and finally in the administration of Sir Robert Borden our province was given continuous service with the modern car ferry as it then was.
We are hoping that history may repeat itself, and that the present Conservative government may be able to provide what is at this time the modern answer to our transportation problems. We feel that the time has come to build a road to the isle. We feel that a causeway across the Northumberland strait, is in this modern age of technology and science, not only feasible but indeed quite possible within a reasonable space of time. The service now existing, while once very adequate, is now incapable of coping properly with the traffic of goods across the strait. It is also a costly operation, causing an annual deficit of about $lf million to keep our ferries running.
We therefore feel that the building of a causeway upon which there may be some reasonable toll would be a self-liquidating project. It would give us a link with the mainland and, better still, it would give the mainland a link with us! Such a causeway would improve our three basic industries and would give a tremendous boost to the economy of our province.
I hope the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Transport will give this their most careful consideration.
I know that my friends and colleagues from Prince Edward Island will not allow anyone to forget their very great interest in this problem. I know of no greater memorial to this government, which we hope will stay in power for a long, long time, than the development of such modern and fine engineering projects, and particularly such a fine boon to the maritime provinces as this particular project which is so close to our hearts.
It has been pleasing indeed to observe the type of legislation which the government has put through. I have been greatly interested in it all, and so have the people of my constituency. The old age pension increase is one example. My personal preference at one time had been for $60 per month as a fair and reasonable amount. But the calculations and the explanations of the minister with respect to the economic and fiscal 

situation struck me as altogether satisfying. I am impressed with the fact that this new increase is 37J per cent over 1949 as against a 23 per cent increase in the cost of living for the same period.
There is one feature about this matter which has a special appeal to the people of my province, and that is the increase in allowable absence from three to six months. Many of our people in years gone by found it necessary to move to the United States, especially the New England states. In this, you see, they were anticipating a certain section of the Gordon report. Many of the older people like to spend part of the winter season with their families in the south. Therefore it will not now be necessary for them to return in the midst of winter. I have already had a great many letters of appreciation on this point.
This is an historic time for a new member to enter the Canadian parliament. The opening by Her Majesty the Queen of course was an unforgettable occasion; the change of government after 22 years of power dominance by one party was in itself something unique. We have also seen something else which I think is new-certainly in degree- in Canadian history, and that is the rapid implementation of election promises by a newly elected government!
We have also seen during this historic time in the record of Canada the end of certain things, and I have a feeling that a great many myths have recently died. We, especially those of us who are young-and I boastfully put myself in that class-had become almost inured to certain myths which had gotten about. I would not say any party did it deliberately,-but they got about. One of those myths was that one party had some sort of monopoly on social welfare legislation. Of course, as any projection back through history or any look through the contemporary record of various provinces under different governments or different political parties would indicate, clearly that is not the case. One could turn to the debate on old age pensions in the year 1907 and there get a cross section of party opinion. There was also the myth of indispensability; that it would be impossible, or at least dangerous, to replace a political party. There also was another myth of invincibility and that well known query "Who is going to stop us?", which had almost passed into the category of a rhetorical question.
There is another very assiduous myth- that national unity adheres to one particular party. I remember we used to be told by so

many leaders of the virtue of voting a certain way for national unity. We had in this house at least a partial demonstration of the falsity of that myth from one of the members on the other side, the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) who gave, I think, a convincing demonstration. He did me the honour of quoting part of an article I wrote. I appreciate his compliment; and while I do not mind for myself being dealt with in this way, I cannot allow to pass any imputation with respect to that great statesman Sir Robert Borden to the effect that he should be adduced as an argument for that which was put forward by the hon. member for Laurier. It would be very immodest of me to practice the art of self quotation, but may I be permitted to put my finger on one very short sentence in the same article, which I think perhaps displays Sir Robert's attitude a little more fully:
(Sir Robert Borden) was not given to pious preachments about his dedication to the furtherance of national unity, but he was nevertheless fully aware of the need for the harmonious interaction of the two great ethnic groups.
Sir Robert Borden did not foster racist divisions, and no man in this country need be ashamed of his Canadianism, whether in this parliament or in the councils of the world, where he strongly and clearly enunciated our national aspirations and became the chief architect of mature Canadian nationhood.
In this party, of which I am proud to be a member, there is no place for any narrowness of outlook on ethnic, religious or cultural lines. We are the great national party of today. We are the only party with representatives from every province in Canada. We have here, and I am proud of it, descendants of many of the peoples whose contribution has made the rich Canadian cultural mosaic. I was always very interested in this great myth of national unity and its association with one party, and am glad to see it has been finally and completely shattered.
One has been impressed also with the impact of the outside world upon our deliberations. The importance laid upon foreign affairs in the speech from the throne has I am sure struck us all; and if one looks back through the debates in the Canadian parliament over the years one sees a gradual development of interest, awareness, information and concern with the outside world.
Indeed, one may say there have been great events even since the speech from the throne was read by the Queen, events so great as to overshadow many of our regular considerations and routine thoughts. Indeed these
mi
The Address-Mr. Macquarrie are stirring and challenging times, and in them petty politics and narrow partisanship seem much out of place. Our earth is now encircled by two man-made satellites, built and launched by the Soviet union. As members of the human species we are thrilled at man's conquest of the lofty heavens, and the imagination warms at the prospect of future triumphs in the vast and illimitable reaches of space. There may be things in store for us which go beyond the fondest dreams of this present moment.
Yet we feel a chill dread about the objects which are swiftly passing through the space around this earth. We wonder if this may be a prelude not to a glorious triumph of man's ingenuity, but a horrible forerunner of man's inability to live peaceably upon this green earth. Whatever else has happened we must admit that we of the western world are late in this field of space conquest. May we not be too late! The forthcoming meeting of NATO at which the leaders of the western states, including our own Prime Minister, will gather may well be a turning point. One is interested in the reaction of people in the western world to this new development. It seems to me we must strike an attitude somewhere between that of panic and that of complacency.
Indeed, linked with this scientific development there is a tremendous political campaign which is exceedingly dangerous. Mr. Khrushchev has said that the western bases in Europe are obsolete. That would be a most dangerous thing to believe. Far from being obsolete they symbolize something which is indispensable to our survival, namely the unity of nations; and I think we will see a great deal more interdependence rather than less.
I am interested in the questions that arise on this very topic from time to time. We must redouble our efforts, and we must turn into practical canons this common ideal which we share. It is not only for parliaments; it is for peoples to meet this present situation. Just the other day in that wonderful newspaper the Christian Science Monitor I read a very simple sentence which strikes me, as does so much of the writing in this paper, as clear, meaningful, and succinct. Speaking of the American people it said:
We prefer a tax cut, we think-to a satellite or a missile-until the Russians have one. And then the heart searching begins.
This is a time, I would say, for some soul searching and heart searching not only among the people of the United States but among the allies of the United States. I think we

The Address-Mr. Sinclair must look very carefully into our educational system so we may meet the present challenge with strength and unity.
From that sense of urgency and common purpose about which I heard the Prime Minister speak at the United Nations some weeks ago may something come which will take us from our present position of second best. These are great and stirring days. May we all be able to measure up to our responsibilities in facing them.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate on the address I must first warmly congratulate you on your election as Speaker of this House of Commons. It is just one month ago that the members of this house unanimously selected you to preside over our debates, and in that month you have amply justified our high hopes. You have shown a very sound knowledge of the rules of the house and, even better, a sound appreciation of the customs of this house. You have displayed a judicial attitude; you have given your rulings with firmness, but alleviated them with a very important ingredient, a sense of humour-a quality I warmly commend to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming).

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: How about applying that comment to yourself?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
You, Mr. Speaker, and I have no common political affiliation, but we have another common bond. Our mutual benefactor expressed the hope that his young scholars would esteem the performance of public duty in their later life as their highest aim. His scholars, on the whole, have done very well in later life, but not too many of them have engaged in public life. You, sir, have amply justified the hopes of Cecil Rhodes by your public service in your own city, in the legislature of your province and here in the parliament of Canada.
While speaking in this vein I think I should also congratulate the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) the two Ministers without Portfolio (Mr. Macdonnell, Mr. Browne) and the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lambert) for the way in which they too have lived up to the hopes of Cecil Rhodes.
It is customary at this time to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address. There was a special interest among the older members of this house in the speech delivered by the mover, because we all knew his father well. His father occupied a very high position in the hearts of this house. He had a very unusual gift, the gift of catching the ear of the house. New members and strangers in the gallery may have noticed at times
[Mr. Macquarrie.l
that when some hon. members get up to speak, though they may be making a good contribution to the debate, others are slipping through the door, reading newspapers or writing letters. Then another hon. member gets up, the house fills, and all listen.
I believe the two private members who were best able to catch the ear of this house in this way were the late Art Smith and Clarence Gillis from Cape Breton South. I think this was because they spoke only on subjects which they knew well. They spoke lucidly, without bitterness or rancour, and enlivened their speeches with an occasional picturesque phrase. That is why we were so pleased to find in the first speech made by the mover of the address that he was following the example of his illustrious father. I am sure that must have been especially warming to his mother, sitting in the gallery.
I am now going to make a reference to the seconder of the address. It is understandable that the attention of older members should have been focused on the mover. I have great sympathy with the seconder, because I was in exactly the same position myself in 1940 when I seconded the address in the reply at the opening of the war parliament. The hon. member who moved the address had a distinguished father who was still in the House of Commons. Well, I think the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Arsenault) and I can console ourselves in this; we may not have been endowed with distinguished ancestors, but both of us are well blessed with a good number of lively, bright young descendants.
Now I should like to say a word to my successor in the ministry of fisheries. During the years I occupied a seat on the government side in the House of Commons I repeatedly said I was sure I had the best job in the government of Canada, in touch with an absorbing industry, an industry of ever-increasing importance in our national economy, assisted by a very able and loyal department and a devoted band of scientists, and having an extraordinarily interesting body of men to represent, the fishermen of Canada. I know my successor will get as much pleasure in grappling with the ever-increasing problems of conservation, protection, marketing, and international control of the seas as I did.
During my period of office the hon. member for Queens took an active interest in the work of the department, and I can assure him I intend to do the same during his period of responsibility. But I wish to make one special reference to his attitude in past years. I went to Russia two years ago to try to arrange for an exchange of information between the Russians and ourselves on fisheries

matters, since we fish the same three oceans of the world, and a year later I had the Russian minister return to see our fishing, and especially to see the advantages of free life in Canada.
We visited Newfoundland first, and then we came to the lovely, green garden of Prince Edward Island. The government of Prince Edward Island held a state dinner, and at the state dinner the Russian guest saw for the first time something new, something they do not have in Russia, a member of the opposition, in fact the hon. member for Queens as he was at that time. I took special pains to introduce him to the Russian minister, and I explained to our visitor that this was the man opposed to me as minister, a man who was going to do his best to defeat our party and who, if this came about, would probably succeed me as minister. Mr. Ishkov agreed politely, but I imagine he was not altogether convinced and really felt that it was a "Potemkin" opposition, as the term they use in Russia goes.
A year has passed since then. I am no longer minister of fisheries and the hon. member for Queens is. I understand my friend Mr. Ishkov is no longer minister of fisheries, either. But there have been a number of other changes in Russia as well since that time. Mr. Molotov is somewhere in Outer Mongolia. Mr. Malenkov is managing a power plant in Turkestan, and Mr. Ishkov is managing a fish plant in Murmansk. Mr. Speaker, I prefer our system because I am still in parliament, not running a fish plant in Aklavik.
This debate on the address does, of course, open the whole field of public policy for debate. I had intended to speak on the financial, trade and employment policies of this government. However, it is a little difficult for me to make such a speech because we have had so little information about the financial, trade and employment policies of this government. Of course we remember the speeches made by supporters of the government when they were in opposition. We remember the many election promises they made, promises which have been singularly neglected in the House of Commons. But we find that the really important policy declarations now seem to be made either in C.B.C. broadcasts or in speeches at Oakville and Winnipeg, and we second class citizens in parliament are obliged to rely on newspaper accounts and questions on the order paper in an effort to find out what is government policy on these matters.
This does, of course, give the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce an opportunity to read once again with relish the speeches they delivered outside this
The Address-Mr. Sinclair house, as they did yesterday, the happy little narcissists. It may give them pleasure, but it is not very satisfactory to the other members of this house.
I had intended to speak especially on the question of unemployment. I did not hear the broadcast of the Prime Minister last week on this subject, but I read an account in the Vancouver papers last Saturday in which the Prime Minister is reported as having said that those who mention unemployment are creating a fear complex, a depression complex, casting gloom in the land. I say this is the most serious domestic problem facing Canada today, and we will spread fear and gloom if we do not discuss this matter thoroughly and frankly in the House of Commons and suggest to the government action which can be taken to curb unemployment in Canada today. We certainly are not going to solve it by ignoring it, by sweeping it under the rug.
Interestingly enough, in the same issue of the Vancouver papers there was a Canadian Press story bearing the headline, "Jobless Expected to Hit 750,000," and it starts off:
A qualified government official predicted today unemployment this winter will likely hit at least 750,000, the highest since the end of the second world war.
This comment was made not by a Liberal member but a qualified government official. Unemployment right now is roughly double what it was in the same month a year ago. In Vancouver last week there were 20.000 registered unemployed, and in the province of British Columbia 40,000. The province of British Columbia is especially vulnerable because we are mainly producers of primary products which are sold on world markets without any protection of the tariff.
There is, of course, one great difference between the condition now and the condition in the thirties. We now do have a floor of social security which was not available to those who were unemployed in the thirties. Unemployment insurance benefits, unemployment assistance paid jointly by the federal government and the provincial governments, family allowances and the universal old age pension all put cash payments into the family group which were not available during the thirties. These, however, are no substitute for employment, and the government this winter must make every effort to maintain the highest possible level of employment.
I said I intended to speak on these subjects but I have changed the nature of my speech because of a matter which has arisen which is of concern to all members from British

The Address-Mr. Sinclair Columbia, members of all parties. It is a problem which concerns us and one in which we are pretty well agreed on the solution, an example of solidarity of British Columbia members irrespective of party which has been seen before in this House of Commons. Since it primarily concerns my riding, although it is also of major interest to the other members from British Columbia, I am going to try to give the house an objective account of the problem; and if I am unfair in my exposition or in my deductions I would welcome interruptions from any of the other British Columbia members on this matter.
The problem is the threatened closure at this time of Britannia Mines in British Columbia. Perhaps I should give a word or two of background. Britannia Mines is one of the great copper mines of the world. For many years it was the largest producer of copper in the British Empire. It is located 30 miles from Vancouver, in a position of some isolation. There is no road connection, and until about a year ago all communication was from the sea. They now have a rather irregular rail service provided by the P.G.E., which is still in the throes of construction in that area.
The mine has operated continuously for 55 years, and there is lots of life left in it. They still have large deposits of low-grade ore. It has always been noted in the mining world as a mine with one of the cheapest costs of operation. Over the years it has given the lead in many new mining methods. The copper is not actually smelted there. The concentrates are sent down to a smelter at Tacoma in the United States. This is an unusual mine and does not go down into the ground; rather it goes up. The mine tunnel comes in from sea level and then shafts go up 4,600 feet into the heart of this mountain, with grade levels every few hundred feet all the way up.
The mine is of special interest to me not only because I am the member representing the area but because it was in this mine that I first started to work 33 years ago. I think we all remember our first job. I remember this particularly well because my father and mother were very much opposed to my going to work in what they regarded as a very dangerous occupation. Finally, when I insisted, my father said to me, "Well, go, but you will be back within a week". If he had not said that I think I would have been back within two days, because it was hard work, but it provided a great training in mining.
It was there, too, I had my first experience with the burden of taxation, a matter which

now interests me much more. British Columbia then had a law which said that every male over the age of 18 who did not support a family had to pay a $5 poll tax. I was not 18 at the time; rather, I was 16. However, in order to work underground I had stretched my age to 18, so I was nicked for this $5 poll tax which I thought was most unjust. It took ten hours of work to pay the $5 poll tax, but of course that was my fault because I had stretched my age to 18. Since my first experience with taxation I have always felt that most taxes would be better spent if left in the pockets of the taxpayers.
The mine has been a great training ground for successive generations of engineers in western Canada. Today the mine is not on the early scale, when it employed over 2,000 miners; but it still employs 800 miners. The whole community contains 1,650 people or 312 families. The monthly payroll today averages just under $300,000 and the monthly supply bill spent by the company in Vancouver averages $150,000 a month. Over the years the company has produced almost $400 million of copper wealth. It has paid heavy taxes both federally and provincially.
Over the last year there have been extraordinary fluctuations in the price of copper on the world markets, the New York export market and the London metal market. There was a high of 47 cents and a low last month of 22.175 cents. The break-even point for the Britannia operation is 30 cents, and when copper declined below this price last May the company started losing money. Last August the price declined to 25J cents, which was 4J cents below the break-even point, and the company began to lose between $70,000 and $80,000 a month.
The company wanted to stay in operation and went to the mine-mill union and asked them to share this loss by taking a 15 per cent cut in wages. The company said if they closed down the mine with the expectation of reopening again it would cost them between $35,000 and $40,000 a month, so they were prepared to assume a loss of that proportion providing the union took a 15 per cent cut in wages as their contribution to maintaining employment in this mine.
The union pointed out that their present wage scale was below the wage scale in most other mines because of the difficult position at Britannia. The union leaders said they did not feel a wage cut at this time was the real answer. It would result, of course, in lower purchasing power for that group, which would be reflected in Vancouver, and it would probably lead to other cuts in other mines around the country and start a spiral of deflation.

The press accounts to the effect that the union had refused to take a wage cut to maintain employment did lose public sympathy. The press accounts were most unfair, because the union did better than take a wage cut. The union pointed out that it was not a cut in wages that the company wanted, it was a cut in the cost of producing copper; and the best way to achieve that, they said, was not to reduce the take-home pay of the miners but to have the miners work longer and harder and so cut the unit cost of production in that way.
This is what the union agreed to do last summer. They agreed, first of all, to forgo taking a 5 cent wage increase which was embodied in a two-year contract signed a year earlier. Secondly, they agreed to work a basic 44-hour week instead of the 40-hour week provided in their contract and under provincial law. They agreed, too, to an alteration in the working time of the miners. The men who regularly worked under what are called portal to portal agreements, who got 42 hours' pay for 38 hours' work, now agreed to work 42 hours for 42 hours' pay.
The most important concession the union made was to waive what are called punitive rates for work on Saturday and Sunday, time and a half pay if they were called upon to work on Saturdays and Sundays. This actually means that the men do not work on Saturdays and Sundays, which after all is what the men really want. Work in a mining community is generally done in continuous shifts, day, afternoon and graveyard shifts, and these shifts rotate during the course of the month. There are few times when all the community is free to take part in a normal sort of community life together, which makes life in Canada so pleasant; but by having a closure such as this, with Saturday and Sunday off because of the extra pay the company would have to pay to keep the mine in operation on these days, they did enjoy on the week ends the community life which is taken for granted by most other Canadians.
The importance of this concession to the company was that they could now run seven days a week, 24 hours a day, and so get full value out of the very costly capital equipment in the mine and in the mill. It was last August that the union and the company agreed to this program, and the price of copper was then 25$ cents a pound. The company and the union agreed to make all these concessions for one year or until copper had climbed back to 30 cents, the break-even point. During the month of August the union leaders met members from all four parties in Vancouver to explain what they were doing. The members also wanted to meet the
The Address-Mr. Sinclair management of the mine. We met them the day following and they explained the situation from their point of view, and assured us that they did want to keep the mine in operation. It was not a shortage of ore but rather the depressed price that was the reason for the present crisis.
After that meeting the members present sent a wire to the federal Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Comtois). Perhaps I should read it:
August 26
As there is serious danger of unemployment in base metal industries because of depressed prices, the following British Columbia members of parliament urge that the federal government be prepared to take emergency action to keep the base metal mines operating.
This wire was signed by Messrs. Taylor, Vancouver-Burrard; Winch, Vancouver East; McLeod, Okanagan-Revelstoke; MacDonald, Vancouver-Kingsway; Irwin, Burnaby-Rich-mond; Hahn, New Westminster; Herridge, Kootenay West; Christian, Okanagan Boundary; Sinclair, Coast-Capilano; Regier, Burn-aby-Coquitlam; and Broome, Vancouver South.
With this agreement the mine continued in operation and the program achieved the success which was hoped for. I do not think there was much enthusiasm at national headquarters of the union for this plan which had been worked out, waiving the agreement, to work longer hours and to cut out over-time pay, but the local union leaders did support it in the hope of maintaining employment.
Because of the men's extra efforts the break-even price of the cost of production at the Britannia mine fell from 30 cents to 27.9 cents a pound and the United States smelter, which smelts the concentrates, joined in to help this program by cutting their smelter costs half a cent a pound, getting the breakeven cost down to 27.4 cents a pound. The company absorbed the remainder of the loss, amounting to about $40,000 a month. Unfortunately, however, since last August world copper prices have declined still further to a low of 22.175 cents, and that meant additional losses to the company of about $80,000 a month or a million dollars a year.
The company have now given notice to the union that they cannot afford to carry on with these losses unless some other form of assistance can be given. It is the feeling of the British Columbia members of all parties that since the company, the smelter and the men have done their best to keep the mine going, the 800 men employed and the community of 1,600 happy, the federal and provincial governments must now assist.
Let me turn to what would happen if the mine were forced to close at the end of the
1116	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Sinclair month. Eight hundred men would lose employment, and with 20,000 already unemployed in Vancouver everyone in our province knows that they have no real hope of getting employment this winter. They could, of course, go on unemployment insurance, because they all have full coverage.
It is more than only this unemployment at Britannia. The ratio of population to primary workers in our industrial towns in British Columbia is about five to one or six to one. At the great pulp and paper company at Powell River and the great smelter at Trail the population is of the order of about six times the number of men actually engaged in the mill. In Britannia it is only two to one because all the other service works, ancillary industries, are in Vancouver; so that in addition to the unemployment in Britannia an equal amount of unemployment will develop in Vancouver because of the closing down of this big industry.
Housing is another problem. The people today are all satisfactorily housed up there. The single men are in good bunk houses, in single rooms, and the married people in 312 houses at rents which range from $7.50 to $20 a month. Last year the company finished 33 new, modern houses in addition, which is evidence that the mine is not worked out. The company would never have spent such an amount of money if the mine were worked out. If the mine shuts down these people will have to be evacuated from their homes because there will be no power, no light, no water and no snow plowing, and they will have to try to find housing in Vancouver, which is a very difficult thing to do these days. It is very costly, and it will drain them of their savings.
Let me take a look at the economic loss if this mine is forced to close. Today these men pay $35,000 a month in personal income tax. If they go on unemployment insurance the very minimum will be $80,000 a month which will be drained out of the unemployment insurance fund. The loss to the people of Britannia means the loss of their homes, the loss of their employment and they will have to move to Vancouver, with the consequent drain on their personal savings. The social loss is the difference between being gainfully employed and idle.
What can be done? One suggestion was that the government should stockpile copper. That is not supported by most mining people. Most of the troubles in the copper industry have come about through governments stockpiling, which drew copper away from industrial users and which then artificially stimulated the price up to 47 cents,


which in turn brought a lot of very low-grade holes in the ground into production. Then the price began to collapse and government stockpiles were dumped on the market which, of course, brought an all-time low price of 22 cents a pound.
Floor prices were suggested. Well, floor prices may be the answer in agriculture and fishing in Canada, but they are not the answer as far as copper is concerned because we produce only 7 per cent of the copper of the world, and a floor price would be of assistance to all the mines, the mines which do not need help as well as those which do.
The third possibility is a direct subsidy to this mine to restore the position to that of last August, when the company and the union reached their agreement. The price of copper was then 25J cents a pound. That would mean a 2J, cents a pound subsidy today. The monthly production of this mine is 14 million pounds of copper. It would cost the government $37,500 a month at the present price to restore conditions to where they were last August. If copper continued to climb in price, of course, that subsidy would decline in amount.
What would this payment achieve? Well, socially it would keep 800 men in this community of 1,650 gainfully employed, living in their present homes, continuing their community activities and producing a needed commodity, copper. They would continue their schools, their churches and their little hospital up there. It would also continue employment in Vancouver for those other industries which supply the mine.
Last week I had meetings at the mine with these workers and their wives, and one thing that struck me about the group there was that they were the oldest group of miners I have ever seen in Canada, and I have visited over the years most of the main mining properties in Canada. Britannia is a stable community 55 years in operation. The miners who were working when I started to work there 33 years ago are still in the company employ; their whole life is there, and if they lose employment at this time there is very little opportunity for them at their age ever to regain work in mining.
Economically, such a subsidy would maintain a payroll of $300,000 a month at Britannia, along with expenditures by the company alone of $150,000 a month in Vancouver. It would mean that the government would still get $35,000 a month in income tax from these employed miners. It would save a drain of $80,000 per month at least on the unemployment insurance fund.

There is a precedent for such aid. In 1948, under similar circumstances, the former government brought in the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act, not to help the mines but to maintain employment in these northern gold mining towns where the mines were finding the fixed price of gold and mounting costs made mining uneconomic. We split the cost roughly between the mines and the government. The program has enabled these mines to stay in operation, maintaining employment and housing. The cost of this program last year was $12 million.
The subvention paid to maritime coal mines is a similar piece of legislation which has enabled the maritime coal mines to stay in operation. Today the Prime Minister announced the extension of that policy to apply to coal mined in the maritimes and used in the maritimes. We supported that. Another example is the guaranteed price for uranium until 1962, which has enabled the great development at Blind River to go ahead, a further example of direct government assistance of this type in the field of mining.
We have many more precedents in other fields. Price supports for farmers are an example of the same principle. Price supports for fishermen have been paid on the prairies, the great lakes and the Atlantic provinces. Fortunately they have never been needed in British Columbia. The subsidy to the railways for the bridge across northern Ontario; subsidies to the steamship companies for maintaining operations on our two coasts, are other examples. The British Columbia members have, in general, supported all these precedents I have mentioned. Last week we all voted, for example, for cash advances to prairie farmers. We want to help the primary producers in every part of Canada. Now we do expect the government to take action to help this particular group of primary producers in our own area.
Yesterday the British Columbia members met the leaders of the miners' union and passed a resolution which was sent to the cabinet, supporting the proposal of the miners' union that this subsidy be paid. Of course the Minister of Finance will immediately raise the question, will this policy have to be extended to other base metal mines? There are two other major producers of copper in the country, International Nickel and Noranda. Both these companies are in a very happy profit position. International Nickel, of course, has the nickel market as its primary source of profit. Noranda has a complex manufacturing industry as well as mines. There are one or two small copper properties, but they have high grade copper
The Address-Mr. Sinclair and are making money. The best evidence of that is that all these other copper mines in the last year have granted substantial pay increases to their miners, in contrast to Britannia where the miners have taken substantial cuts. The director of the mine and mill union assures us he knows of no other copper mine in this predicament. So far as the lead and zinc mines are concerned, their problem will arise next year if the United States does raise the tariff on lead and zinc.
We all know the tendency of people to lean on the government in time of trouble. The Britannia miners, however, can come to the government in this respect with clean hands, because they have tried to help themselves. If it had not been for the continued drop in copper prices the arrangement they worked out last summer would have been sufficient. It is true that another government has a responsibility, because the provincial government has the primary control over mining. The provincial government receives a royalty, of course, on all mining production, and they get a 5 per cent sales tax on all purchases. I feel a joint program should be worked out between the federal and provincial governments.
I believe we British Columbia members regard this as a key case, not of mining but of employment. If government action is taken in this key case it will certainly do a great deal to dispel the gloom and despair of many people who are unemployed, and others in British Columbia who are fearing unemployment. We have acute unemployment problems in British Columbia.
I think the satisfactory solution of this particular problem could well be the signpost of government action. If the mine closes down I am afraid a lot of people in British Columbia will regard this as a return to the thinking of the thirties, when the relief camp was the only answer to unemployment. If, however, direct government action keeps this mine in operation, in conjunction with the sacrifices already made by the company, by the smelter and by the miners, it will be a very positive approach. It will be heartening to all British Columbians. It makes good sense economically, because a $37,000 monthly subsidy keeps $35,000 in income tax payments rolling in and saves $80,000 per month in unemployment insurance benefits.
It is because of this that the British Columbia members of all parties have sent a letter to the Prime Minister supporting the presentation which was made by the union to the government this morning. I think I can speak on behalf of them all in urging

The Address-Mr. C. E. Johnston the government to give prompt and favourable consideration to this positive approach to help unemployment in British Columbia at this time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on this occasion I should like to speak about two matters. One is unemployment and the other is related to it, that is, some of our industries in Canada. During the session this year members from all parts of the house have been indicating to us and to you, sir, the ever-growing unemployment problem. The speech to which we have just listened was an excellent account of some of the unemployment conditions occurring in British Columbia. I believe this situation applies not only to British Columbia but to the whole of Canada.
I am afraid the reason for this condition is not any local situation, because the condition is genera] across the whole country. Of course it is my opinion, and I think the opinion of authorities across Canada, that one of the greatest causes contributing toward this unemployment problem is the financial system under which we are operating; that is, the present financial system followed by the Conservative party and which was carried on by the Liberal party. It is the tight money policy which is causing a great deal of the disturbance throughout the whole of the nation.
In this regard I should like to refer to an article which I read in the Gazette of Tuesday, November 12, 1957. The headline reads "Montreal Economist Raps Juggling; Ottawa Tight Money Policy Contributes to Recession". The article reads:
Canadian monetary policy "has certainly contributed to the recession we now are in," J. R. Petrie, Montreal consulting economist, said today in an address to the annual tax conference of the Canadian tax foundation.
"I do not," he added, "place the whole blame for this recession on monetary policy, but a

determined enough credit squeeze can take the froth off any boom, and cause a downward swing in economic activity."
Then farther down in the article he said:
"It is true that many prices are still rising, but if this be inflation it is not the kind of inflation we had five years ago when the pressure on prices was caused by a shortage of goods in relation to demand. There are no shortages now."
A little further on he said:
Maintenance of tight money is not going to solve the cost-price-push. While I am not satisfied that easier money will stop this recession now, I am convinced that the maintenance of existing monetary policy will aggravate both its amplitude and existing.
Then he ended up in this way:
I am in full sympathy with maritime business and political leaders who protest against tight money.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that when authorities of that kind attribute our recession-I suppose they hesitate to use the word "recession"-to the tight money policy, considerable attention should be given to that matter. The members of the Social Credit party in this house have on many occasions gone into this problem. The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) has dealt with it in detail on several occasions. Not only this year but in years gone by he has pointed out the dangers of such a monetary trend and indicated that the result would be universal unemployment.
Of course that is the thing that is happening now. From the hon. member who has just spoken we have had an account of how the mining industries in British Columbia are collapsing. How the lumber industry has collapsed has been pointed out by others. Then we have the example of secondary industries closing across the country, creating more unemployment; and particularly we have the coal industry in western Canada, of which I will speak in a little bit more detail later on, closing and that too causing a continuation and accelaration of the recession.
It cannot be said that this unemployment problem we have been facing is of a local nature because it has been unquestionably pointed out:
Canada's unemployment total, usually stable at this time of the year, jumped by 20,000 during September to 194,000. The jobless represent 3.2 per cent of the labour force, almost double the 1.7 per cent of a year ago. At the same time there were 5,854,000 persons with jobs, a drop of 103,000 from the previous month's record total of 5,957,000.
This is not the opinion of myself. It is borne out most emphatically by a release which we received the other day from the Department of Labour and the bureau of

statistics dated October 23 which has this to say, and I am quoting from this report:
The number of persons without jobs and seeking work, which usually remains relatively stable at this time of year, increased by 20,000 during the month to 194,000, representing 3.2 per cent of the labour force, compared with 1.7 per cent a year earlier.
Then down further they have this to say about this alarming situation:
Unemployment in September was still considerably higher than last year in virtually all local labour markets.
That is the statement which was given by the government, or by the Department of Labour and the dominion bureau of statistics. This unemployment is being experienced, as I indicated, in British Columbia, in the Atlantic provinces, in the central provinces and in western Canada. I have literally hundreds of newspaper clippings which I have saved over the last three or four months and which indicate that this problem is ever increasing. Let me just give you one or two. I have many more, but I do not want to take up the time of the house by reading them all. Here is one I have from the Albertan of Monday, September 16, 1957. It reads in part as follows:
Initial and renewal claims for unemployment insurance benefits in July totalled 117,107, an increase of 55 per cent over last year's corresponding total and an advance of 30 per cent over the June figure.
You will note, Mr. Speaker, that the increase has been most rapid since June 10.T I am not implying that the present government is responsible for all this situation, but I am pointing out most definitely that they have now had an opportunity to tackle this problem but that so far their policies have not been any different in this respect than those of the Liberals who preceded them. Here is another clipping which is headed "Fears Bad Lay-off in Construction," and which reads in part as follows:
Ottawa (CP)-Raymond Brunet of Hull, Quebec, past president of the Canadian Construction Association, says one-quarter of Canada's construction labour force of 550,000 may be out of work between December 15 and March 31.
Then here is another one from my own province. It is from the Calgary Herald of Wednesday, October 21, 1957. It is headed "Cement Plant Lays Off 97" and it reads in part as follows:
Shortage of orders led to a lay-off of 97 workers Tuesday at the manufacturing plant of Canada Cement Company Limited in Exshaw.
The measure was taken to reduce the number of shifts being worked at the plant from three to two daily. Duration of the lay-off is not yet determined.
As was pointed out in one of the articles I read, this recession is different from the one during the hungry thirties because then
The Address-Mr. C. E. Johnston there was a shortage of goods. There is no shortage of goods now. Certainly there are inflated prices, but there is no shortage of consumer goods. One of the causes of the increase in prices, of course, is the tight money policy which was started by the Liberals and pursued by them, and which is being continued without interruption by this present government.
If we are going to look for the causes of this general recession across the country we had better look to that cause at which all the authorities are pointing, namely the financial system in this country. The premier of New Brunswick, Mr. Flemming, indicated this not so long ago when he was pointing out the deplorable economic conditions in his province. The Social Credit members have pointed it out on a number of occasions here in this house. It is time the government began to take some cognizance of this fact and see what can be done.
I think one of the reasons for the unemployment problem, and which has its bearing on the tight money policy, are the unusually high interest rates which are being charged industry. Of course those interest rates always go into prices, thus making it much more difficult for our people in this country to buy the goods which are produced. Then, of course, as unemployment continues prices remain high, fewer consumer goods are produced, more people are on the unemployment lists and so the vicious cycle continues.
One of the reasons we have been able to hold our head up as high and as long as we have, of course, is the tremendous amount of credit buying that has taken place across this country. Credit buying has amounted in the last year to about $2f billion. That credit buying is certainly not going to help the economy for any length of time, because when people are short of purchasing power, when they lose their jobs and have their incomes cut and then are obliged to revert to credit buying or buying on the instalment plan, their prices are greatly increased. The interest rates on this credit extension in a great number of cases have amounted to anywhere from 5 per cent to 50 per cent, and the ones who are being hit the hardest are those who are in the unfortunate position of having no jobs at all or on fixed incomes.
What have this government been doing to solve the unemployment problem? Have they a policy which is going to solve this serious condition? My mind goes back to the action this government took just the other day when the seamen in the Montreal area went on strike for higher wages. I am not at this point taking any part on the side of the

The Address-Mr. C. E. Johnston unions or anybody else's side. I am just pointing out the condition as it exists. The seamen went on strike for an increase in pay. The government immediately brought forth what I suppose they considered an appropriate solution, and so they permitted eight vessels of Canadian National Steamships, a government owned crown corporation, to be transferred to foreign registry. The ships will be registered at Port of Spain, Trinidad. The company stated that by doing this they will be able to compete with other shipping companies who are hiring foreigners on their ships at lower rates of pay, and this government is a partner in that action.
Perhaps some of the members of this house have never been to the West Indies. It was my privilege to visit that area about a year ago, and I am going to say to the members of this parliament that Canadian National Steamships will have no difficulty whatsoever in getting lots of cheap labour anywhere in the West Indies. When we made that trip throughout the West Indies we stopped at nearly all the ports which were doing business with the commonwealth, and on every occasion when we stopped at these ports the docks were just lined with workers, hundreds of them, seeking employment. I have never visited a place where the economic conditions were as low as they are in the West Indies and, make no mistake about it, Canadian National Steamship Company, as far as employment on these eight ships is concerned, will be able to get a lot of cheap labour.
The distressing part of this whole thing is that here we have the government of this country in an effort to solve their internal unemployment problems saying in effect to the working people of this country, "If you do not lower your standard of living and accept lower wages then we will get foreigners to take your jobs." I do not think anything could be more deplorable. The government is saying in effect to all industries in this country that one of the ways to lower their costs and, incidentally, to increase their profits is to hire foreign labour. You might as well go out and lower your immigration barriers and allow foreigners to come in and absorb the work which Canadians are doing.
That is not the solution. What is going to be the result? The result will be, as in the seamen's strike, that all these men will be thrown out of work, their families will no longer have the pay cheques coming in each month, and their standard of living will be reduced considerably-almost to nil-with their purchasing power gone.
They will be buying less consumer goods. Of course, there again is a vicious cycle; less purchasing power, less consumer goods

used, less production from the industries and then, naturally, more unemployment. That is not the way, surely, to solve our internal unemployment problems, and the government must accept a portion of the blame because they were the ones who permitted this action to be taken. I cannot help but think that this action on the part of the Conservative party smacks very largely of what happened in the hungry thirties. We had unemployment problems then, and when the unemployed of western Canada decided to come down to Ottawa and complain they were stopped at Regina by the police. I will not go into the treatment they were given; I will not expand on that but unfortunately, although it may be a coincidence, that was the time when the Conservative government was in power under the former prime minister, Right Hon. R. B. Bennett.
Is that going to be the policy of this government? It certainly looks like it, because it smacks most strongly of the iron hand for our unemployed. I think there could be some alleviation of this problem, but before I go on to a different angle of my talk may I call it one o'clock.
At one o'clock the house took recess.

Mr. Speaker, I was about to branch out into another topic, namely the subject of industry in Canada. I think one of the things which would help solve our unemployment problem in this country would be for the government to embark on a determined plan to decentralize industry. This question has been brought before the house on a number of occasions in days gone by but too little attention has been paid to it, with the result that most of our industries are concentrated in the two central provinces of Ontario and Quebec because of a number of factors which give these two provinces an advantage with regard to the employment of people as compared with other parts of the country.
One of the factors which has prevented industry from locating in the Atlantic and western provinces is the discriminatory freight rate system we have in this country. We in the province of Alberta have felt this discrimination keenly over a number of years. We have the highest freight rates in Canada, and industry is therefore hesitant about moving to that part of the country to establish factories. It is impossible for industries in the west to compete with industries located in central Canada while

they have to pay such exorbitantly high freight rates. It is not a good thing for the country as a whole, either from an economic standpoint or from the point of view of national defence, that industries should be concentrated so heavily in the two central provinces. It would be an easy matter for the enemy to ruin us in a few months with the help of modern weapons now at their disposal.
Another reason it has been difficult to establish industries in western Canada is the tariff structure. Industries which have settled in central Canada enjoy a very high degree of tariff protection while industries in other parts of Canada have very little. I am thinking especially of the agricultural industry in western Canada. The agricultural industry has no tariff protection, or very little. Certainly there is no tariff protection with regard to wheat. The farmers must sell their wheat on the open market and buy all the goods they require on a protected market.
This is particularly true in respect of our coal industry, and I want to spend a little time in considering the coal industry not only in western Canada, Alberta and Drum-heller in my riding, but in all other parts of Canada as well.
It is true that both the present government and the government which preceded it have been applying the principle of subsidies. Quite clearly the application of subsidies alone has not been sufficient to enable industries in other parts of Canada to compete against those of the two central provinces. That is particularly true in the case of coal. As I say, the government's policy has not changed. It is true that in one or two instances there have been increases in subsidies. The Prime Minister mentioned something of this sort this morning while he was speaking about the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, and I expect the position in those two provinces will be somewhat eased as a result. But we in the west have found that the subsidies which have been provided are not sufficient to keep our coal industry alive.
The coal industry is essential to Canada, particularly in wartime. This was brought home to us during the last war when the United States government refused to ship us any coal, and we had to depend upon our own resources. Had we found ourselves then in the same position as we find ourselves today, we should have been in a very difficult situation indeed because today our mines are rapidly closing out not only in the west but in other parts of Canada as well.
When I speak of tariffs I am not unmindful of the fact that a certain amount of
The Address-Mr. C. E. Johnston tariff protection is good. What I am complaining about is the unequal tariff protection which results in a situation in which almost the only industries which enjoy protection are the large manufacturing industries concentrated in Ontario and Quebec. The coal mining industry has no such protection, yet little has been done about it. I have myself brought the question before the house many times and other hon. members have done the same, but so far nothing has been done which would stimulate the growth of this industry.
Only the other day, on November 4, the Calgary Herald carried a report of a speech by Mr. C. V. Daniels, president of the Calgary chamber of commerce, in which he said that the Alberta coal industry is in an extremely depressed state because of declining markets for its products in Canada and elsewhere. Mr. James J. Part, the city manager of Drumheller, also pointed out the need for decentralization of industry and for some assistance to be given to the coal mining industry in that area. He pointed out that Drumheller is an excellent spot-and so it is-for the establishment of industry if some of the obstacles to which I have referred were removed. Down in the valley there we have the largest supply of coal in Canada. In Alberta there is over 48 billion tons of coal, yet our mines are being closed year after year at an ever-increasing rate. As I say, we have plenty of coal in the Drumheller area-cheap coal, too, for industrial use. We have electric power; we have a mighty river running through the area; we have gas and oil, all the inducements which would encourage industry to locate there. If some attention were given by this government to the decentralization of industry and to the changing of our present unfair tariff structure, a great deal would be done to encourage such relocation.
I noticed that the other day when I asked the Minister of Transport about this question he seemed unsure about whether there was any undue discrimination in Canadian freight rates. The minister has been here a long time and has heard a good many of us speak on this question in the house, and if he does not know that now he had better get acquainted with his department soon.
The other day I wrote a letter to the dominion coal board asking for some information on this subject, and they produced some figures from the bureau of statistics and sent them over to me. With the permission of the house I should like to have this short table put on record in Hansard.

What is the result of all this? Because we are using so much coal imported from the United States we are giving the people of that country employment in their coal mines, while at the very same time we are destroying our Canadian mines and putting our own people out of work, thereby aggravating the unemployment problem here in Canada.
A subsidy offers some relief, but it is only a palliative. Two per cent of Ontario's total requirements last year came from the western provinces and 98 per cent from the United States. Forty-two per cent of Quebec's total requirements came from the eastern provinces and 58 per cent from the United States. Ontario is our natural market. I think some attention should be given to the Canadian coal industry.
As I say, a subsidy is not enough and it will not solve our problem. We could very easily see to it that imports of coal from the United States were cut down a little. Last year they shipped in over 22 million tons for sale in the Ontario market. If we were to give the Canadian mines only 2 million tons of this 22 million which is imported from the United States it would not hurt the United States economy at all, and would serve to bring back to life our own Canadian market.
What we need most of all is a national fuel policy, one that will provide employment for our own people and protect this

country in time of war. If we were to reduce our United States imports by just two million tons as I suggest this would give our own people the employment that is so greatly needed to keep our coal industry alive. It would revive the western coal industry and also give the Atlantic provinces the stimulus required to revive their coal industry. In short, let us make Canada for Canadians and not so much for foreigners.

Mr. Speaker, as a new member, may I congratulate you on the honour conferred upon you by this house in choosing you as its Speaker. It is an honour which assuredly reflects the high regard which hon. members have for you. Your thorough knowledge of both languages will no doubt prove a great asset in carrying out your responsibilities, and this ability is more particularly appreciated by us, who speak both French and English. May I also point out that, since the opening of this session, I have been agreeably surprised to find that so many English-speaking members, especially on this side of the house, have shown remarkable familiarity with the French language. Let us hope that their number will increase with the growing realization, by every one, of the advantages of being bilingual.
I should like to quote from an article which appeared in a bulletin entitled "Industry" published by the Canadian Manufacturers Association, and which I am translating as follows:
"French and English are in fact the two official languages of Canada, but the proportion of Canadians who can speak both is unfortunately small, barely twelve per cent. Of the remaining 88 per cent, 67 speak English but no French; 20 understand French and not English, and one person in a hundred speaks neither language.
It is imperative that we do better than that before we can genuinely feel that we have reached the status of an indivisible nation. There should not be a single Englishspeaking Canadian who does not have some knowledge of French, no more than there should be a single French-speaking Canadian unfamiliar with English; because a Canadian who, for some reason or other, lacks a good command of both official languages of his country is not only the poorer, in the matter of language, but he is, in fact, divorced from several million of his fellow-citizens, and all the obstacles to an efficient and true unity are in this way, much more real. At this time, when students of all ages have registered for a new term in our schools, 96698-72
The Address-Mr. Lambert colleges and universities, it seems particularly fitting that we give some thought to those matters."
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to congratulate your deputy, the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Courtemanche) whose geniality and poise so eminently fit him for this position. May I also, like all those who preceded me, tender my congratulations to my good friend the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) for his contribution in moving the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Though he hails from a locality scarcely known to the people of Edmonton, he has been to me, for many years, a colleague for whose judgment and experience I have the highest regard. By the same token, I commend the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Arsenault) for his excellent speech when seconding the motion of the hon. member for Calgary South.
It would indeed be ungrateful on my part to pursue my remarks without expressing my sincere thanks to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) for appointing me parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes). Like so many others in this house, I am a veteran of the second world war. While I do not claim to be an expert in the matter, I may say that I take a great interest in national defence. I acknowledge my shortcomings, my limitations, but I should like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that I could not have found greater satisfaction than in working under the direction of the hon. Minister of National Defence. As was stated previously in the house, he can be described as being unfailingly a gentleman in the true sense of the word. I am very grateful to the hon. members opposite for referring to him in those terms.
Mr. Speaker, it was more than sixty years ago that my father, then eighteen, left his birthplace in the county of Terrebonne, and went to Edmonton, which at the time was a little known still less developed district. A little later, his family followed him. Young though it is, western Canada has its traditions. My grandfather was Conservative member for St. Albert in the last parliament of the Northwest Territories, in Regina, from 1901 to 1904. Most of this constituency is now part of the one I represent. The village of St. Albert, a monument to venerable Father Lacombe, that pioneer missionary of western Canada, is now on the threshold of promising development, after lying dormant for nearly fifty years. A great construction and modernization project is contemplated, and I should like here to wish my electors from St. Albert every success in their undertakings.

The Address-Mr. Lambert
I should like to point out that Alberta has some sixty thousand French-speaking citizens. However, no more than about 4,000 of them live in my constituency, which has a total population of nearly 120,000. The fact remains that I was elected in Edmonton West because I was bilingual, because, you see, where I come from, we all feel united. In voting for me the people of Edmonton West did not feel they were supporting a member of a party which practices disunity. So I would suggest to the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), who, unfortunately is not here at the moment, as well as to the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) and others, to go out west and find out for themselves about the views of the French-speaking population there.
Mr. Speaker, they would be amazed to learn that those people do not share the opinion expressed the other day by these gentlemen. Though a small minority, we have lived in co-operation and harmony with our neighbours. If those hon. members would only lift their noses out of the mud with which they are trying to cloud the waters of national unity, they would realize that the Conservatives are recognized as a national party which is consistently working for the unity of this country. The enthusiasm with which the hon. members opposite greeted the inanities we heard the other day about national unity, and which were repeated more recently in Joliette, just shows to what extent the principles held by the Liberal party are bankrupt. The same applies to the emphasis laid on the so-called Diefenbaker-Duplessis axis. For want of something better, it has become the cry of despair of the Liberal party.
If I may venture a suggestion, let them come out of their shells; let them travel in the rest of Canada. They will be welcomed with kindness, especially out west, for our hospitality is well known, but I assure you, Mr. Speaker, they will listen to a few home truths.
People come over from Quebec each year to visit us, and in my opinion they realize that harmony can prevail among people of different races and different faiths without their indulging in snide remarks or bickering. Liberal members have but to look at us, sitting on this side of the house, and they will see an example of the national unity of races and religions. The Conservative party derives its strength from all sources. We are Anglo Saxons, French Canadians (and it should not be forgotten that we got 575,000 votes in the province of Quebec on June 10), Ukrainians, Scandinavians, Italians, Chinese ... Is that evidence of disunity?

I had the opportunity to congratulate you, Mr. Speaker, a few moments ago on your election as Speaker of this house. May I be permitted a moment of personal gratification. I join you, sir, in this house not only as a fellow member of Hertford college, Oxford, but with considerable satisfaction as one of that body of Rhodes scholars who are members of this house. Amongst these scholars we number you, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton), the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne), both members of the treasury benches.

and I should like to welcome back to this house the hon. member for St. John's West-and on the other side of the house there is the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair), also a former occupant of the treasury benches. Recently we were pleased to read that another Rhodes scholar had achieved distinction in the person of Mr. Justice St. Germain, whose appointment to the supreme court of Quebec province will be welcomed by all.
I would say also that I have been more than ordinarily surprised at the large number of Rhodes scholars who occupy high positions of trust in the government of Canada. Indeed, if one looks at the list of Canadian Rhodes scholars and assesses their achievements as a whole, one cannot have but a feeling of satisfaction at the fulfilment of the trust and expectations of the administrators of the Rhodes trust in approving their choice of scholars. You, sir, have been secretary for the Rhodes trust of this country for many years, and you know whereof I speak.
If I may be permitted, Mr. Speaker, I should like to urge upon the members of this house that, should the occasion arise, they recommend that young, promising students of this country strive for Rhodes scholarships in order to gain an education that, in my very humble opinion, is on a par with, and in many respects and in the minds of many superior to that which can be obtained anywhere else. In so doing they may assure to this country in some measure a source of leaders as well in industry as in the professions and public life. It may be said that Canadian Rhodes scholars as a whole fulfilled the vision of Cecil Rhodes in establishing these scholarships.
As a new member of this house, Mr. Speaker, I of course had my first impressions from the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I am astounded and somewhat disappointed in the attitude of many of the members, particularly those opposite. We have heard recita-

tions of serious ruin in so many constituencies. Surely this country has not reached its present eminent position because of all these disasters, either actual or predicted, about which some members appear to be concerned. I would have thought that it was the function of a member not only to have the nature and status of his constituency in its proper perspective, but to tell the rest of the people of Canada what his own people were doing rather than what they were not doing. It is not in the spirit of pessimism that we must approach our functions as members of this house.
I am not by that saying there are no problems, some grave and some of a more minor nature, which exist in this country today. Problems have existed in the past; they exist now, and they will exist in the future. We were not born into a paradise, a sort of Shangri-la, where life would go on serenely at all times. The fortunes of this country and its achievements have not been built by Canadian people who, every time some difficulty arose, cried to the heavens and had their members run complaining to parliament asking what was the government doing about it.
The constituency of Edmonton West, Mr. Speaker, is one of the most heavily populated in this country. There are upwards of 120,000 people living in a relatively small area, composed of 85 per cent urban dwellers and 15 per cent farmers and small holders. The rural area is in the main a good productive area, the better part of which lies in the milkshed of the city of Edmonton. There are no vast farm holdings there, but the farmers of my constituency are an industrious group of men and women who have had the initiative to cope with their problems and get on with the job.
The city of Edmonton, of which I represent only a part, has made tremendous strides since the end of world war II. The population has more than doubled so that now in the metropolitan area of that city it numbers almost 275,000. This great growth has not been without problems and grave difficulties, to some of which I shall refer later. But again, Mr. Speaker, that growth, like that of the rest of Canada, has not been the result of appointing ourselves the death-watch beetles of our economy.
This growth of Edmonton, and of many of the towns in its area, has been in part the result of the developments in the oil and chemical industry. Notwithstanding the credit that may be assumed by certain people for the prosperity of Alberta, there is no doubt in the mind of anyone that this prosperity is in good measure the result of resources 96698-72i
The Address-Mr. Lambert placed there by divine Providence. There has been generally good administration of all those resources. By this I do not mean to say that it has been the best of administration and due solely to the abilities of that political party which has administered the affairs of Alberta during that time. In my humble opinion it would have taken knaves and fools to do worse.
However, notwithstanding the claims of the Alberta government that it has done so well in the past ten years and that the provincial government is in the equivalent of a debt-free position, this position has been achieved at the expense of the municipalities. Great and serious demands have been made on the municipalities because of the vast expansion that has occurred in Alberta, yet the revenues of those municipalities have not been commensurate with the needs that had to be fulfilled and fulfilled immediately, not at some indefinite time in the future.
