What was done? A plan was formulated by the builders and real estate agents to meet the needs of Edmonton. Along with the representatives of industry I was very pleased to bring this plan to the attention of the government.
The answer to this and no doubt similar proposals from others was quick action in making available $150 million for National Housing Act lower cost housing. To date we have dealt with legislation to implement cash advances for farm-stored grain, increases in old age pensions and supplementary allowances, blind and disabled pensions, war veterans allowances and other changes for the benefit of veterans. These were emergency measures, the need for them having accumulated for a long time. They were but the first instalment in the fulfilment of a long legislative program of this Conservative government.
This is a prelude to the implementation of a national policy for the benefit of all Canada. This is not a promise of fulfilment tomorrow. In this national program I submit we must not be overly preoccupied with props and palliatives. Let us not neglect the foundation, the pillars and the roof of our economic structure. Let us not provide pillows and pads to cushion every fall to the detriment of national initiative and individual responsibility. We have heard a great deal about the rights of citizens, but what of the corresponding duties and responsibilities? We have heard little or nothing of them. I would ask those who seek to emphasize rights to dwell also upon those duties, to pause and reflect upon them most carefully-those duties of citizens and those duties of members of this house-not to any one particular group of our citizens but to the people of Canada as a whole.
Mr. Speaker, there are many matters upon which I could dwell and urge upon the government. I spoke previously of a national policy. This would include the development of that vast hinterland of the great northwest. There in that great majestic country of mountain, lake, forest and endless Arctic waste lies untold wealth. Therein lies part of the great future of this nation. If this generation is not to see the complete fruition of that development, let us pass on to our children and generations to come the legacy of a plan well conceived and well initiated. To northern Alberta will come a great measure of the benefits of such a program of northern development, and upon the people of that region devolves a greater than proportionate share of responsibility for the carrying out of that program. I feel sure that enlightened selfinterest will prevail, and that they shall not be found wanting.

Mr. Speaker, for years there have been representations made to the government that an alternative trans-Canada route be built through the northern section of the western provinces, using the Yellowhead pass. These pleas have apparently fallen on deaf ears. I would submit, Mr. Speaker, that the present position of our national highway system is indefensible. We have wasted years in the past by inactivity, by a refusal to look to the future. The whole of the blame is not to be assumed by the federal government; the provinces concerned must too take part of the responsibility.
The present route utilizing Rogers pass is, I submit, the least preferable of any route. It is exceedingly costly to build, and there is some considerable doubt as to its providing a year-round route. On the other hand the Yellowhead pass has a much lower gradient and has not the snow conditions prevailing on the presently proposed route. From a national defence point of view it is essential that as soon as possible we develop alternative routes through the mountains to the Pacific coast. The degree of vulnerability to which we are exposed is frankly frightening. The few lines of communication that we have could be so easily put out of commission. Then from a tourist and a commercial point of view the arguments in favour of alternative routes are unanswerable.
Alberta is at the apex of the freight rate structure, and we should like to be able to ship out our products and bring in products from both west and east by the cheapest means possible, by road transport if that be the preferable way. There is no reason why we should have to depend upon long trips over United States highways to bring our goods from western Canada to eastern Canada and vice versa. It is ludicrous that people from northern Alberta who wish to go to the lower mainland in British Columbia or to the fine mountain resorts in the interior of that province should have to travel by United States highways. I need not point out that Canadian tourists spend far more in the United States than do United States tourists in Canada. I would say today, build our roads within Canada so that Canadians can travel in Canada if they choose to do so; so that they may spend their money here and get to know their country better.
This ability to get around one's own country might perhaps do something to dispel that lack of knowledge we have of one another's area. At the present time I find there is a regrettable ignorance of conditions in eastern Canada on the part of the people of the west,
The Address-Mr. Lambert but perhaps not to the same degree that there is among the people of central and eastern Canada about the west.
In this connection may I be permitted this observation. As a western member in Ottawa I can find nothing, in fact less than nothing, in the newspapers of Central Canada about either the west or the far east of this great country. I do not know, Mr. Speaker, whether there has been erected a sort of paper curtain at the great lakes, but there are important things of interest to both citizens and members of government in central Canada happening in other parts of Canada. I do not know whether or not the reason for the situation to which I have referred is preoccupation with local affairs. However, if I may be permitted to do so I should like to suggest to the press of this country that they could do a great deal more for the unity of this country and the knowledge we may have of one another if they concerned themselves a little bit more with the events taking place outside the particular provinces or city in which a newspaper is published.
I hope I do not appear to be too critical, but I offer that suggestion as something in the way of constructive criticism. I believe that a newspaper has qualities which permit it to be more useful in that sphere than other means of communication. Radio and television, if not heard or seen, are missed, but a newspaper can be put aside and can be picked up tomorrow or can be passed from hand to hand. The printed word remains. I feel that perhaps in the not too distant future we shall have what I should like to consider a truly national press. I merely make that suggestion as a plea to have more news of Canada as a whole.
Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, we heard from the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Broome). He pointed out some very serious criticisms about Trans-Canada Air Lines. Well, frankly we in Canada have been put in a most ludicrous position because of the monopoly which exists in favour of Trans-Canada Air Lines. In a recent number of the Edmonton Journal a story was written of two residents of Alberta, one from Edmonton and one from Calgary, who when coming back from the Orient had to land at Edmonton because the airport terminals in British Columbia were fogbound. Perhaps the members from British Columbia would not admit that, but fog does exist out there. However, they landed at Edmonton airport and were told they could not terminate their journey there; they would have to wait until the fog lifted in Vancouver when their aircraft, at some indefinite time in the future would go to that city, then take their chance on Trans-Canada Air Lines coming back to Edmonton

The Address-Mr. Lambert and Calgary. In addition, they were not permitted to make personal contact with their relatives. They had to speak to them on the telephone, one of these relatives down in the lobby and the other the traveller up in a room. They were not permitted access to their relatives because they had not been cleared by the immigration authorities.
There, I would suggest, we have bumbling of the worst sort. Why would the immigration authorities in Edmontoin not be able to examine those people and clear them? All that stems from the monopoly accorded to Trans-Canada Air Lines, which prohibits Canadian Pacific Airlines from landing at intermediate points in this country on its international route.
Frankly, how ridiculous can we get?
Yesterday we heard a speech by the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Lesage). With a great roll of thunder the hon. members of this house were assailed as to the so-called lack of policy by this government. I believe the hon. member called it government by postponement. In the most, to my mind, chameleon-like intonations he recited chapter and verse of the alleged and actual problems which face us today; but he will have to admit, as will most members opposite, that these problems existed prior to June 10. They were there. If the administration of that time did not know about them then they ought to have known about them. Either way it was dishonest. They did nothing about them if they knew of them, and as I say, if they did not know about them then they should have known. Theirs was government by ignorance, either wilful or blissful.
Yesterday we heard not one word of constructive suggestion; no alternative was proposed. Is that the policy of the official opposition or is it, as someone said on the other side of the house, their policy to see that those on this side of the house carry out the government's policy? I would have thought that the role of the official opposition, the responsible role of the official opposition, was to offer constructive criticism and alternatives, not merely to criticize for criticisms's sake or with an eye to certain forthcoming events.

I think it is essential that real consideration should be given to this subject. When we had a period of six years for re-examination of an income return I think many people whose incomes were being reexamined found it difficult to explain many of the items which were in the return. Consequently, if this period could be reduced to two years as requested in this resolution I feel it would place the taxpayer and those people who are concerned with returns of this nature in a much better position to explain anything which might be asked of them.
There is another reason why I think this should be done, and done as soon as possible. We find that if the period goes back too far, normally the person whose income is being re-examined will find it necessary to get legal opinion, engage an accountant and so on, and any expenditure incurred in trying to have the income tax file cleared is not allowable as a charge which can be assessed as a deduction in the following year.
These are some of the things to which I think people are objecting, and so I commend these considerations to the government for examination and I am sure that when the Minister of Finance brings down a budget, as he has stated he will do, and when changes in the Income Tax Act are being considered this resolution as passed by the women's institute of the region from which I come will receive serious attention from the government. I can see no reason why this proposal should not be accepted because, on examination of Hansard at page 715 of the same date, January 28, 1957, I note that ten of the ministers who are now sitting with the government, five of the parliamentary assistants and others supported this motion. I note, too, that some of the ministers were not present when this motion was called. I certainly think, however, that the proposal would receive a majority in the cabinet in favour of the passage of this Income Tax Act change.

Mr. Huffman
There is a further item I should like to bring to the attention of the government.
I think it was put very clearly by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Campbell) when, speaking in this house on November 11, he said that Ontario wheat growers were in a worse position than the growers in the west as far as price is concerned.
During the month that this house has been in session I have asked the government if they would bring forward legislation pertaining to the resolution No. 8 on the order paper. That resolution reads:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to establish a system of guaranteed prices for certain agricultural commodities to be named therein and to provide that prices may be guaranteed for any other agricultural commodity or commodities as named from time to time by the governor in council-
Some other words follow in connection with the establishment of a committee, and so on.
Now on the occasion on which I asked for this legislation to be brought in, before the debate on the address had been concluded, I felt that my request was a sincere one, and I was more convinced than ever that there was a good reason for making it after the hon. member for Lambton-Kent had made his remarks the other day. Last Friday the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) asked the leader of the house if this legislation would be proceeded with before the address in reply to the speech from the throne was concluded. I thought it was a rather unfortunate remark when the leader of the house said that the hon. member for Essex East and myself were only seeking publicity.
I would like to say that that was not the reason for referring to this motion and seeking to have it brought forward at the earliest possible date. I felt there was just as much reason for bringing this forward as there was for bringing forward the resolution with respect to cash advances. We were not interested in obtaining publicity, which was the term used by the house leader, and this definitely was not the reason for our raising the question.
One other reason for making this request was that almost as soon as the present government took office back in June there were representatives of farm organizations coming to Ottawa to lay before the government their requests for assistance of one kind and another. I believe the reason that the hon. member for Lambton-Kent spoke on wheat was because representatives of the wheat growers organization were in Ottawa. It will be necessary to have a change made in the Agricultural Prices Support Act because

wheat is specifically excluded from that act at the present time. It was my hope that we would have notification on the order paper of the government's intention to amend the act at this session in order to include wheat. In addition, representatives of other primary producers and the growers of different commodities have come to Ottawa to present their claims. I believe the farmers in the Fraser valley and the primary producers in the eastern provinces have equally as much right to be heard and to have legislation passed to benefit them as have the prairie wheat farmers especially when we postponed the debate on the throne speech in order to bring forward as early as possible legislation concerning cash advances.
The other day I asked the government if the request of the sugar beet growers would be entertained. My reason for raising this question is that shortly the sugar companies will be negotiating contracts for the coming year. When the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand (Mr. Charlton), who is now parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness), spoke last session, as reported at page 3319 of Hansard, on April 9, 1957, he said:
We have always stood for a flexible price support program with prices based on a formula and stated well in advance of the production period.
At that time the house was discussing the amendment of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) requesting establishment of adequate support prices.
The government has had all the necessary information that could be placed before it for the introduction of such legislation because the provincial ministers of agriculture have been here as well as representatives of the various farm organizations. I am sure that farm organizations across the country have placed this problem before the government. I feel that the longer we delay some action of this kind the more difficult it is going to be for the sugar company to get the number of acres under contract that many of us would like to see. I hope this legislation will be brought before the house at the earliest possible moment and that certain provisions contained in this resolution will be spelled out in such a manner that every one will know exactly what is going to happen with respect to a certain commodity. We would also like to know exactly what commodities are going to come under the Agricultural Prices Support Act.
From time to time there has been genuine concern in the rural communities because of the action that has been taken on previous occasions by hon. members opposite. We recall that on at least two occasions a parity

price motion has been before the house and on those two occasions hon. members opposite supported it. On another occasion during the past session the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort (Mr. Bryson) presented a motion regarding 100 per cent parity, on which occasion our friends who now form the government voted against the motion.

Under section 9 of the Agricultural Prices Support Act there is a form of parity. This section provides that the board will step in and buy farm products when the prices fall below the level of other products and that they will endeavour to maintain the prices of farm products at a fair relationship to the price of other commodities. This is the policy that has been followed since this act was passed in 1944. This act was in effect when this country underwent the transition from a wartime to peacetime effort and in many instances it certainly provided the balance which was needed in the industry. Possibly there were times when this stated floor price was not as high as we would like to have had it but at this time I hope the government will spell out in clear language exactly what it has in mind so that our people can follow the example recommended by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture when he said we should have this well in advance of the production period.
Many primary producers organizations are meeting at the present time. I have had the farm union representatives call on me at my office and I know that the Ontario Federation of Agriculture met in Toronto last week. I was notified that this organization passed a resolution asking that the government consider the extension of cash advances to include primary producers in all of Canada which is the same position I adopted in this house.
The Address-Mr. Huffman
When the present Prime Minister spoke on April 9, 1957, as reported at page 3305 of Hansard of that date, referring to the Agricultural Prices Support Act he said:
-that a policy has developed that is used only in extreme circumstances, and that its present uses are not providing the necessary floors to maintain a responsible, profitable agriculture . . . we believe that action must be taken and taken at once.
Therefore I commend to the government at this time the words of the Prime Minister and the words of the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture who is in my view the listening post for agriculture in eastern Canada. I trust that the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand will use his influence with the Minister of Agriculture in seeing that the primary producers in every part of the country will receive consideration as early as possible. There are other quotations that I might use in regard to this very problem but I feel that I have said enough along this line.
At this time I would like to make a suggestion to the government in this form. For some years past we have found that storage has been a problem in this country. There is a regulation in the Income Tax Act to the effect that if a company or an individual wanted to build storage they could apply to the minister of trade and commerce, whose department gave approval to the project. If that project was approved, accelerated depreciation was allowed and it could be depreciated at 33J per cent a year, or in full in three years. I would like to suggest that at the present time the terms of the act might be extended to individuals who would like to build storage in which they would be able to maintain their commodities at home so that they could be fed in market channels when they were needed and in that way there would be provided one of the better balances that are necessary in agriculture especially.
At the present time the Income Tax regulation works in this way. If the construction is of steel the depreciation is 2J per cent so that it takes 40 years to get full depreciation. If it is of wooden construction the depreciation is 5 per cent so that it takes 20 years to get full depreciation. Therefore, there is not a great deal of encouragement for anyone to build the storages because of the depreciation allowances in the Income Tax Act. My two recommendations have to do, first with the Income Tax Act as it applies to the length of time for re-examination of files; and, second, accelerated depreciation. I commend them to the government. I think it is a case of live and let live; but live and let live is never as good as live and help live which is a part the government can play.

Mr. Speaker, it has not been my practice in the years that I have been in this house to join in the chorus of congratulations which this debate seems to draw forth. I have been quite content to let the leader of this group speak for all of us in the felicitations that he has extended during the course of the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, as he has done at this session. However, on this occasion there is one word that I would like to say. As a previous speaker has already pointed out, it is exactly a month ago today that this house chose the hon. member for St. Paul's to be the Speaker of the House of Commons in this twenty-third parliament. I was more than satisfied that day that we were making a wise choice and I am sure all members agree with me that the intervening month has proven the wisdom of our choice. Indeed, His Honour has occupied the chair with dignity. He has been fair and firm in his decisions and, as another hon. member has pointed out, he has exercised the good humour that is required in the pursuit of his duties. We are satisfied that His Honour will do a good job. We give him our support and we wish him well.
It has been our practice as a C.C.F. group in parliament, during the years that we have been here, to welcome good legislation no matter who brought it in and even if there were some who thought that that legislation was stolen from our platform.
In that same vein we have welcomed the legislation which parliament thus far has been given an opportunity to endorse, particularly the legislation respecting cash advances to prairie farmers and the legislation in the social security field. We shall continue to give our support to beneficial legislation that is brought in by this government, or any government that may be in power at any time. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, so long as we are in the opposition we shall remember that it is the job of an opposition in this democratic parliament to point out the shortcomings of the government in power and to prod that government into the implementation of its own promises and into the implementation of other measures that are for the good of the people of this country. I can assure the members of the present government that we in this group will continue to fulfil that role even as we sought to fulfil it during the days when the Liberals sat to Mr. Speaker's right.
In my remarks this afternoon I intend to point out some of the serious shortcomings of this government which are already showing up and I intend to do what I can to prod


this government into action along certain lines. Perhaps at the start I should remind hon. members opposite, both those who are in the cabinet and those who are on the back benches, that they delude themselves if they interpret what happened on June 10 as meaning that they were elected on their own merits. What happened on June 10 was that the people of Canada voted against the former Liberal administration. The people of Canada were disappointed in the slowness with which that former administration moved in such fields as social security and the people of Canada were apprehensive with respect to the dictatorial manner in which the previous government was handling parliament. Therefore, on June 10, Canadians went out and voted against the former government. The result of that vote was that no party had a majority of the popular vote in this country and no party had a majority of the seats in this House of Commons. In other words, this present government, with a minority of the seats and with a minority of the popular vote, is in power more or less by default. This government is still in the position of having to prove its worth to the Canadian people and I suggest that there are signs that it is not going to succeed in that effort. In fact, I suggest there are few signs of that effort even being made.
I know that it is a very popular type of speech for hon. members opposite to make to list the things which have been done already in this session of parliament which have had the endorsation of the entire House of Commons. May I point out that all of those items that have been put through are items that simply had to be passed because of the way in which the votes were cast on June 10. Those were issues that were discussed from the Atlantic to the Pacific in that election campaign. There was deep concern over social security measures. There was deep concern over the position of the prairie farmers. In fact, the government was just the instrument for bringing before parliament some of the things for which the people of Canada voted on June 10.
But after you have looked at those items of legislation, beneficial and acceptable as they are, I suggest that all you have from this government opposite is a bits and pieces program, without any general over-all policy or philosophy. Where does this government go from here? Where does it go when it has finished putting on the statute books the items that have been mentioned in the speech from the throne? Where does this government go in certain important fields which I shall indicate in a moment? In fact, I suggest that one of the reasons the government

opposite is trying its best to lay the groundwork for an early election is because it does not know where it is going after a few more items have been passed.
Apparently the election may come sooner than some people think from a remark that was dropped this afternoon by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Hodgson). He interjected to say to some of the Liberals opposite him that some of them would not be here at the next session. If he knows what he is talking about, that means the plan is for an election before the next session of parliament. Perhaps he is right for, as I say, the government is running out so far as its bits and pieces program is concerned.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in order to be quite specific when I make the statement that this government has no over-all policy, that this government does not know where it is going, let me list a number of fields in which any government worth its salt should give leadership. I will take only a minute to talk about trade because it has been talked about very effectively by members in other parties on this side of the house, and it was spoken to very forcefully, very effectively, a few days ago by my colleague the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny). The government does not know whether or not it wants to shift 15 per cent of our trade from the United States to the United Kingdom. The government does not know where it stands with respect to the United Kingdom's proposal for a free trade area between this country and that. The government does not know whether or not it wants to take the necessary steps to develop trade with China. In the whole field of trade, this government simply does not know where it is going, has not got any over-all policy.
The same remarks are true of the field of finance. The government uses constitutional excuses for not telling us, through the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), what that minister is saying in his conversations with the governor of the Bank of Canada. But it is quite clear that the same Minister of Finance does not know whether or not he favours tight money or easy money; does not know in what direction we should be going in terms of the control of finance, in terms of control of investment, in terms of social planning so far as finance is concerned. In fact, I suggest that those opposite are completely at sea so far as the real, basic factors in financial policy are concerned.
The government is likewise at sea in the field of taxation. They do not know where they are going and they do not know what they are doing. The Minister of Finance told the press last July that there would be a 96698-734
The Address-Mr. S. Knowles budget at this session. Can we get out of him now whether or not there is going to be one? I defy anyone to determine, from what the minister has said in answer to questions, whether or not there will be a budget at this session. He probably does not know because the bringing down of a budget involves some changes in taxation structures. During the election campaign the Conservatives promised they would raise the tax exemption levels. I suppose they are sufficiently familiar with income tax matters to realize that if they raise the income tax exemption levels without making any other changes they will be giving the greatest bonanza to those in the upper income brackets. Perhaps they realize that if they are going to do all the things they are proposing, and at the same time raise the income tax exemption levels, they are going to have to find some other sources of tax revenues and that would raise the question of what they should do about taxation in the upper brackets; that would raise the question of what they should do about corporation income tax. I say, Mr. Speaker, those at your right are at sea in this field; they do not know what they are doing. This is a time that calls for leadership in these fields. There is no sign of it from this bits and pieces government across the way; this government that can use high-sounding words but cannot give any leadership, cannot tell parliament when anything is going to be done or even what is going to be done.
The same remarks are true in the important field of federal-provincial relations. There is going to be a conference and it is only a week or two away. Can we get out of the government any indication of what its plans are? All we can ascertain is that some of the provincial governments are going to put a rather terrific squeeze on this government, and our fear is that some rather unfortunate changes in federal-provincial tax-sharing arrangements might be made which could have the effect of lessening the unity of Canada so far as taxation matters are concerned. This is an extremely important field and the federal government should be giving the lead. No government can give the lead in a matter like this unless it knows where it is going and this government, despite all the bits and pieces of fine legislation we have had at this session, does not know where it is going.
I might mention housing. The government and its supporters like to stand up and talk about that move to increase the amount of money available under the National Housing Act, which was already there under the previous legislation. But there has been no suggestion that this government realizes that

This is an important economic and social problem affecting our people. This is something in which there should be leadership, but at a time when we need such leadership we have in power a government that is there only by default, not because the Canadian people put them there but because the Canadian people put the Liberals out. I shall not take the time to go into agriculture because that has been fully debated in this house, and my colleagues have spelled out the situation. It is clear again that this government is prepared to bring in certain palliatives to assist the farmers in western Canada in getting their yearly income, such as it is, spread a little more evenly throughout the year. However, this does not solve the basic problem of the price-cost squeeze so far as the farmers are concerned. It does not solve the problem of enabling the farmers to receive their fair share of the national income. I suggest that here is another field in which this bits and pieces government is completely lacking in any over-all policy.

turn to the field of labour. Here, too, there is a woeful lack of leadership. During the election campaign there were many speeches made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) and others as to what a Conservative government would do in the field of labour. They were going to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act; the benefit period was to be extended to a full year and benefits were to be increased. These were not items that were going to be attended to some time a few years from now, these were things that the Conservative party suggested they would go at immediately. Now when the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) is asked about amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act he gives us that same old answer the Liberals used to give us, he is studying the matter.
This government promised the labour people of Canada in the course of the election campaign that there would be an overhaul of the national labour code; that the conciliation


procedures would be speeded up. Does the government not realize that there is every possibility that within a matter of months it may be faced with a number of labour disputes?
Surely hon. members are aware of the situation that may possibly develop between the non-operating employees of the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway. Is this government going to do the same as the last government did, namely wait until the dispute has reached a crisis and then in the middle of the crisis, change the rules? Oh, they did not like it when the previous government did it. But this present government has no policy and is giving no lead in this field. It does not know where it is going here any more than in any other situation.
The government talked about legislation to provide for minimum wages and for annual holidays with pay and for statutory holidays. The Prime Minister made speeches like that, particularly during the early part of this year and during the election campaign in various parts of Canada, but so far this session we have had only one measure touching any of these fields; and even in that one measure the government has fallen short of the request made to them in all sincerity and in all faithfulness by the Canadian Labour Congress as well as by other labour organizations. It looks to me as though the government does not know what it is all about and that it does not understand labour matters any more than it understands some other matters. Certainly it is not giving any lead in this field. I cannot say we have bits and pieces; we have just one bit so far as labour legislation is concerned.
The same thing is true in the social security field. I know that hon. members opposite think it is wonderful what they did in a short space of time by way of amending various statutes that had been on the books for a few years, in some instances, or many years, in others. But I submit to you that there was no real analysis of the situation as to the amount of the pension necessary for our senior citizens and others. I submit to you that the $55 figure which is now the law of the land does not measure up to the Prime Minister's assurance to the old people of Canada that, if his party came to power, they would receive a pension to meet today's cost of living.
I submit to you that, in the light of the increase in the gross national product since 1949 when the figure of $40 was set, there was a complete lack of policy, a complete lack of fairness and a complete lack of justice to give to our people only that much increase

when the increase in the gross national product has been something over 80 per cent, which means that the increase in old age pensions should have been brought up to something of the order of $75 a month. There is no real policy on the part of the government, no leadership, no understanding of the basic issues, no concept of the social factors involved in this matter. It is just a government that likes to indulge in words, that enjoys being in office, that enjoys the fact that it is administering the affairs of the country, enjoys the fact that it is able to bring in some bits and pieces of legislation but which in the long-run has no over-all policy and indeed has no policy with respect to these individual items.
Where is it in the field of transportation? It has some real problems facing it in connection with the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships. There will be problems arising because of the relationships between the railway employees and the two major railways in this country. There will be problems arising because of demands for increases in freight rates. Here is a field, the field of transportation, in which some real understanding and some real leadership is called for. But we have a government that does not know where it is going at all.
Where is it with respect to air transportation in this country? Hon. members are aware of the interesting exchange we had this morning with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) with respect to the application made by Canadian Pacific Air Lines to compete with Trans-Canada Air Lines on the Montreal to Vancouver route. Hon. members are aware of the attempt of the cabinet ministers to be extremely careful and extremely cautious on this point. Yet at the same time from back benchers on the Tory side of the house there is carping criticism of what they refer to as to the T.C.A. monopoly which, I suggest, is one of the fine examples of something that is important in this country, namely public ownership of a natural monopoly. Not only do they not know where they are going, but ignorance in this field means that they are likely to slip back.
Where are they in the field of pipe line policy? They do not know. They have had to appoint a royal commission to find out what should be done in that field. In the meantime many questions are left unanswered, despite the fact that hon. gentlemen opposite joined with us in 1956-I know it was at the end of the debate but nevertheless they joined with us at the end-in calling for public ownership of the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Company so that the money to be made out of this natural monopoly might accrue, not
The Address-Mr. S. Knowles in millions to private individuals but to the people of Canada as a whole. Where are they going now in pipe line policy? They know no more in that field than they know in these other fields. They are a bits and pieces government that comes down with a few items of legislation, all of which are good, but it has no over-all philosophy, no over-all understanding as to where it is going.
What is its policy with regard to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation? We have ideas as to what they might like to do as regards the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. At least it is not going to be sold, at least not for $50 million. The Prime Minister made that point clear. But where are we going with respect to the C.B.C., with respect to the Fowler report and these other important matters?
Another field in which this government is very much at sea is in the field of defence. I leave the matter at that for the moment because I want to come back to it in a few minutes in connection with my remarks. Likewise I suggest that it is at sea in the whole field of external affairs and on that matter too I will say something in just a moment.
But before I do so I should like to come back for just a moment to the question of the old age pension and say that the people of Canada have found it quite a disappointment that a party which gave the impression to the country during the election campaign that it stood for $60 a month-that impression was given very carefully; it is hard to pin it down, but the impression was given- should now try to buy our older people off with $55 a month. We still feel that under present conditions the pension should be $75 a month, but the least that the party opposite should have done was to implement the promise it made, namely that if elected it would bring in $60 a month. As hon. members know, a situation developed in my own experience that made it necessary for me to be home in Winnipeg for a few days, in fact while these social security measures were being debated. As one would expect, I picked up comments with regard to this matter from a number of people. I say to you quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, that I thought people would be pleased, that that would be the only kind of comment I would get, namely that the people would be pleased that the pension was to be increased to $55 a month, that people would forget that we had asked for $75. Mr. Speaker, I had many a phone call and met many persons on the streets of Winnipeg who expressed nothing but disappointment that this government which gave the impression they stood for $60 tried: to buy the old people off with $55 a month..

The Address-Mr. S. Knowles That is not leadership. That is not facing up to the needs of the day. That is not being faithful to the promise that these old people would have a chance to keep up with today's cost of living. This is the work of a bits and pieces government that does not know where it is going and that is not conscious of the real needs of the people of this country.
When are we going to get action with regard to the pensions of superannuated civil servants? When are we going to get some action with regard to Canadian National Railways pensioners, particularly those who are still on the basic pension of only $25 a month? Those are matters on which hon. gentlemen opposite, along with us in this group, had a great deal to say when they were on this side of the house. But now that they are on the other side of the house, what do we find? Oh, we get words. We get the same kind of assurances that the Liberals used to give us but we still get no action. These people are supposed to be satisfied with the general legislation that has been passed, but that is not good enough.
There is another item concerning which this government is showing that it is not a cabinet that is prepared to give leadership and that is in this whole field of health insurance or more particularly hospital insurance in the terms of the legislation that was passed in this house last April. I read again today some of the debates that took place last April. The Conservatives who at that time sat over on this side of the house insisted, along with us, that amendments should be made in that legislation to extend its coverage and to make possible its early implementation.
The Conservatives in the early part of 1957 wanted the six province requirement reduced to five provinces so that this legislation might be brought in with the least possible delay. Well six provinces have now indicated their agreement so we have got over that hurdle.
These people who wanted action when they were on this side of the house are now on the other side where they can do something about it, but they tell us no agreements have been signed with any of the provinces and they are now even quibbling over the meaning of the words "in operation" and "in force". This looks to some of us as though an attempt is being made to stall the implementation of the hospital insurance program just as long as it is possible to do so. I have no doubt Premier Frost will be remembered and that his desire to have his plan in operation by the first of January, 1959,

will not be overlooked, but Premier Frost and Ontario are not the only premier and only province in Canada.
We submit that those provinces which already have plans-British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and some of the others- are entitled to their share of federal money just as soon as six provinces have their plans in force so far as legislation is concerned. That is the way the act reads and I defy the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) or anyone else to put any other interpretation on the legislation which was passed last session.
I remind the house that the minister of health in the province of Nova Scotia is calling for a clear statement as to where the government stands. The minister called for that information by letter dated September 30 and again on October 16 he referred back to the previous letter asking for a statement, which he seems unable to get. When the premier of Saskatchewan sought information on the matter in a letter during the summer the Prime Minister told him that he could not make a statement prior to the opening of parliament in October. Well parliament has been in session for a month and we still have no statement. For a while we were told it would not even be put on the agenda of the federal-provincial conference on November 25 and 26. Now we are told it can be discussed if the provincial premiers want it discussed.
Well, Mr. Speaker, these gentlemen across the way may be proud of the fact that, as they think, they won the election; they may be proud of the fact that they are in power but they are not giving leadership in this important field of health; they are not giving leadership in any field, and I submit to the government members that unless they do come through with something in terms of leadership on this important item their days on the other side of the house are numbered.
There is another field in which we are not getting leadership from across the way. We have moved into a new era-let us admit that; it is a simple statement of fact-since the day when the first sputnik was launched. It is a new phase of life so far as mankind is concerned and yet these people opposite think of everything that has happened, so far as the Russians are concerned, as only a military challenge. Well it is a military challenge all right. It should make us think about our so called defences but I submit that the tremendous advances which the Russians have made in the scientific field call for far more than just the kind of panic that causes us to reappraise our military

defences: it demands that we re-examine our whole approach to a number of very important aspects of our way of life.
One thing it calls for is a tremendous expansion of what we spend and of what we do in the field of scientific research. This is something which is supported not only by those of us in this party but by members of other parties who have placed resolutions on the order paper. As a matter of fact a few days ago I noticed in a newsletter of one of the banks in this country-certainly no socialist organization-a strong plea for tremendous increase in the amount of public money to be spent on both basic and applied research.
I say, too, that if we are going to meet the challenge which the Russians have given to the world we have got to do something about our whole educational situation in the west. No longer should we hold back on this question of the federal aid to education because of some of the niceties which have been brought out in debate in years gone by. Yes, we have the British North America Act which gives the provinces full control over education, and that fact must be respected, but the opportunity for education in all of the 10 provinces of Canada to be raised considerably by means of financial aid is here for any government that will give the leadership required. The last one did not do it; this one has shown no sign of it. It looks as though in the next election the people will have to vote for a real change instead of merely the fictitious change they got on June 10.
I suggest also we have to do something to try and capture for our free way of life the enthusiasm and the zeal of our people in the way the Russian regime has captured it for their dictatorial way of doing things. To me one of the ominous things in the world today is the fact that that regime has been able to stay in power for 40 years. We do not brush it aside by simply saying it is a dictatorship, that it is a form of slavery. Any regime that has been able to stay in power that long has somehow been able to captivate its people and to get its people feeling that life under that regime and life in pursuit of the objectives of that regime is worth while. I submit that is one of the reasons they have been able to make these advances in science.
When we ask for adequate social security, for adequate old age pensions, for a proper national health program; when we ask for the social and economic planning necessary to eliminate unemployment altogether and when we ask for public ownership of some
The Address-Mr. Maclnnis of our great national projects, we are suggesting that we should have the kind of society under the banner of freedom in which every citizen of the land feels he is a participant in the things we are doing. We can do these things to a much greater extent than can be done under a system of slavery or dictatorship, but as yet we do not seem to have the leadership that calls forth that sort of zeal and enthusiasm.
I urge that there be such leadership in this country and that this government realize that during the time it is in power it should be giving some of that leadership. There should also be leadership in the field of external affairs. I have in mind an editorial in the Vancouver Sun of which copies I believe were sent to all of us. I think it is time we shook off the Dulles era of diplomacy; it is time we shook off the notion that you can deal with the Russians by insulting them; it is time we shook off the notion that when they produce their intercontinental ballistic missile our only answer is a speed-up of the arms race on our side.
I am conscious of some of the things which were said by some of us in a debate a few years ago. We were a minority but we expressed the fear that a certain course of action which the west was taking would be a case of going beyond the point of no return. Maybe we are beyond that point and if so the time has come to realize that the Russians, even with their present superiority over us, are just as afraid of annihilation as we are and just as afraid of world war as we are. Surely the time has come for the west and the east to sit down as equals, to realize that we have tremendous scientific possibilities and to try to work out a basis of living together, using this modern scientific knowledge to build a better world for all mankind.
This is not an age in which to be frightened; this is not an age in which to panic into more defences and into an arms race; it is not an age in which to give a country like Canada only a bits and pieces program. This is an age in which the government should be giving leadership. The last one did not do it and this one shows even less signs than the last one of giving the leadership we so sorely need. It may be that the Canadian people will have to avail themselves of the next opportunity-the next election, which no doubt is not far off-to put in power a party with vision-a party prepared to give leadership in times like these.

Mr. Speaker, in rising in this house for the first time let me congratulate you on your

The Address-Mr. Maclnnis appointment to such a high office. I wish also to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Rising to speak in this house is somewhat different from rising to speak in my own local union but I am proud to say- and this is no reflection on parliament but a boost to my union-that the big difference is all in favour of the union, because nowhere in all of Cape Breton would you find a group of men who would continuously denounce and criticize any business before them and then rise as one entire bloc in their places and vote for it.
I must apologize to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill). We are sorry that we who are the so-called backbenchers of this party do not act in accordance with his expectations. We have no intention of following the example of the backbenchers of the previous government. I further feel that since I have been elected to represent Cape Breton South I should be lacking in my duty if I were to sit idly by while an hon. member in opposition thinks he is qualified to speak for the maritimes, when he and his party have failed to act in that respect. I am perfectly willing to listen to anyone on national issues, but I still feel that maritimers are best qualified to speak on maritime problems, and we are elected for that purpose.
I would remind the house, that during world war II the constituency of Cape Breton and, in particular, the town of New Waterford, had the highest percentage per capita of volunteer enlistment of any part of this country, and yet since the war this achievement has been met by a complete lack of appreciation by the previous government.
Miners who during the war were considered so important to the war effort that they were "frozen" to their jobs, and even taken out of the service to work in the mines were made jobless without any consideration from the past administration.
You will forgive me if I say that I enjoy the predicament in which the official opposition now find themselves. It is very similar to that of the Cape Breton miners during the past 12 to 15 years. The thought of another election to them is somewhat like the threat of mines closing down to the Cape Breton miners.
The opposition speaks of giving the present government an opportunity to carry out their election promises. This comes rather inappropriately from them in the light of a statement made in this house by the member for

Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) as reported at page 183 of Hansard of 1957:
We do not feel we are a broken-down party, and I believe those sitting on the other side of the house will be convinced that that statement is correct within a few months.
I say to you, sir, their contemptible attitude is one they intend to continue as long as it fits in with their political purposes, and it indicates we can look forward to a change following their convention, at which time they hope to re-organize and re-group.
Everybody in this house knows that the maritime provinces have had, and still have, grievances due to economic difficulties that the previous government would do nothing about. The hon. member for Inverness-Rich-mond (Mr. MacEachen) admits this, and he had this to say as late as Monday as recorded at page 972 of Hansard of November 11, 1957 as follows:
The present Progressive Conservative leader and his candidates, as I say, capitalized upon this peculiar and legitimate grievance, and presented a commitment to the people of the Atlantic area prior to the election of June 10.
Since he himself considered it a legitimate grievance, I would remind him it was also an old one which he and his party failed to recognize and deal with.
He drew the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) in respect to coal subventions to the attention of this house, and he referred to the throne speech in which it was stated that this government was prepared to pay subventions on the movement of coal for power purposes in the maritime provinces. Let me now draw to the attention of the house what his leader had to say in respect to the maritime problems according to a press report:
If it was found that power could not be produced at reasonable prices, the Atlantic provinces would have to do without.
He further stated that eventually coal would be too valuable a material for production of synthetic products to be used as a fuel. He did not want to see coal centres turned into ghost towns, but he would not encourage any immediate substantial increase in coal production. It would not be fair to future generations in the maritimes who would greatly benefit from the increased value of coal as an industrial raw material. If federal developed thermal power aided Nova Scotia coal mines, that was incidental. His concern for a ghost town of the future is most touching. I would also draw the attention of the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond to page 974 of Hansard when he quoted a statement made by the Prime Minister in Minto, New Brunswick:
There should be and must be a subvention on coal transported within these provinces for power purposes.

Well, he had his answer this morning. I should also like to draw the attention of hon. members to the attitude of the former minister of fisheries as contained in a press release from Westville, Nova Scotia, on November 25:
Westville, March 25. The mayor of this Nova Scotia mining town feels Hon. James Sinclair, dominion fisheries minister "should have been chased out of the province for what he said about our coal industry" during a visit to the province.
Mayor Alfred Matheson was one of several civic and union officials in Nova Scotia's coal producing areas to criticize remarks made by Mr. Sinclair in a recent address at Antigonish, Nova Scotia.
The fisheries minister was quoted as saying that uneconomical coal mines must eventually close and that in view of a tremendous demand for labour in Canada there is "no point in subsidizing an industry merely for the sake of providing employment".
Mr. Sinclair later told a press conference "the only value of a subsidy is to tide an operation over a difficult period, if in the end you see that it is going to be of value".
I may say, sir, that the former prime minister figured that coal would be very valuable in the future. The press release continues:
"Mines are not like fisheries. They do not work out. and there is no sense in trying to keep a mine alive which you know is going to be permanently uneconomical."
In his reply, Mayor Matheson said that wheat farmers, gold mines, railroads and even fisheries receive subsidies. He also referred to unfair competition to Nova Scotia miners from the importation of 33 million tons of American coal a year.
"We're fighting for another coal mine in Pictou county and we shouldn't let some western politician come in and knock us down", Mayor Matheson said.
United Mine Workers Locals have also criticized Mr. Sinclair's statements.
Union officials at Princess local in Sydney Mines termed the statement, "brazen, and a black eye to organized workers in the coal industry in this province".
William Carey, a hoard member of United Mine Workers, told union members that "to have the Minister of Fisheries come into Nova Scotia and dictate a policy cannot and will not be accepted by the coal union".
Mr. Sinclair, who arrived in Vancouver today, declined to comment on Mayor Matheson's statement.
He reiterated his previous remark that there "is no point in keeping these marginal operations going with subsidies on the grounds that they provide employment when there is such a shortage of labour all over Canada".
I do not wish at this time to elaborate on the situation of the coal industry in Nova Scotia. With the change in ownership it is hoped that the Avro Company will improve the position in Cape Breton. But I do say now that a pressing problem for the miners of Cape Breton is the matter of wages and working conditions. The miners of Cape Breton have sacrificed much these past years. One has only to go back to the Sir Andrew Rae Duncan royal commission report to realize what they have contributed to the industrial life of this country. At that time
The Address-Mr. Maclnnis the commission felt that the miners who were the backbone of the company were entitled to a raise. Company policy was that they were part of an over-all industry and as such could not receive any rate. Today however the company has reversed its position and our miners are still suffering. I might point out that if the company had continued its previous policy the miners would be in a much happier position and the losses suffered at some collieries could be easily absorbed by the over-all profits and further closings could be thus eliminated.
I would now like to make a few brief remarks for the benefit of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate the former minister of citizenship and immigration. I have representations from groups in my constituency that would prove the administration of that department under the hon. gentleman was nothing less than discriminatory. This could be further supported by the opinion voiced by the Canadian Labour Congress. On Tuesday the hon. member saw fit to criticize the makeup of the present cabinet. I find this a strange attitude indeed considering his own position in the last cabinet. This hon. member in his own written opinion is an expert on fish; that is in his own written opinion.
I also wish to comment on the remarks of the hon. leader of the C.C.F. party. To my surprise this party that makes so much of the slogan "The Political Arm of Labour" through its leader had this to say as reported at page 855 of Hansard of November 7, 1957:
May I ask the Prime Minister this supplementary question. Is it not a fact that the Saskatchewan government has been on record to the effect that it would bear the whole cost of the electrical installation and some other costs, but that since the government is to assist in the development of electricity in the maritimes Saskatchewan does not expect to be discriminated against by the government of Canada?
The hon. member was referring to the commencement of construction of the South Saskatchewan river dam. The hon. member says in effect that Saskatchewan would pay the whole cost of electrical installation, but if the dominion government is to assist the maritimes in power development it must at the same time aid Saskatchewan. This is the crudest kind of political horse trading I have ever heard of. We supported legislation to help western wheat growers but we did not do it on a quid pro quo basis in return for comparable benefits- to the maritimes; we supported it as proper and necessary legislation to assist western farmers. I suggest to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) that he should take a

The Address-Mr. Maclnnis similar stand in respect to legislation designed to assist us. Where would we get with legislation in this house, I ask the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, if every member said, "Yes, I will vote for this legislation if you will do the same thing for my constituency". It would mean putting dominion politics on the auction block of local self-interest.

Before continuing with my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say how very much I regret the circumstances which made it necessary for the Leader of the Opposition (St. Laurent) to announce some weeks ago his decision to retire from the leadership of the Liberal party. I believe it is no exaggeration to say that no one in Canada in our own times has commanded greater respect from those like myself who have been associated with him in the Liberal party, as well as from his political adversaries, and indeed from Canadians all across our country. I cannot help thinking, Mr. Speaker, that in the future, when we come back to look more objectively than we do at the present time upon the period in which he presided over the destinies of Canada, we shall realize even more fully than we do today the greatness of the contribution he has made. I know it was with a heavy heart that he reached the decision as to his retirement; but I hope he will derive much satisfaction not only from the general regret that is being felt in all parts of the country, but also, and perhaps more particularly, from the fact that during the eight years or more he was Prime Minister of our country Canadians came to regard prosperity in Canada as a normal and natural state of affairs.
I think, Mr. Speaker, they had good cause for that state of mind because the last eight years have been without parallel in the history of Canada. Year after year, in almost every field of endeavour, new records have been established that have made Canada the envy of the western world. In support of those views I could cite many figures but I shall merely point out that during that period of eight years Canada's gross national product increased from $15.6 billion in 1948 to an all-time high of nearly $30 billion in
1956.	To all intents and purposes the gross national product had nearly doubled during this relatively short period which ended on December 31 last.
What was the situation at the end of June,
1957,	when the present government took office? I think the question merits some attention because already hon. members on the government side of the house are talking of the economic conditions which then prevailed in much the same terms as they would have used if the new government had inherited a first-class depression. Perhaps these same members are not unconscious of
the fact-perhaps it is an unfortunate one- that in the minds of many Canadians economic depressions are still closely associated with Conservative governments. But what are the facts of the matter, Mr. Speaker? I am going to cite only a few figures to show that despite the sombre description given by Conservative members, the present government inherited a prosperous economy.
First, corporation profits before taxes for the calendar year 1956 were the highest in history, and corporation net earnings for the first six months of 1957 were greater than those for the corresponding period of any previous year except 1956. In fact, corporation net earnings for the first six months of 1957 were $2,249 million compared with $2,254 million in the first six months of 1956; that is to say they were only one-quarter of one per cent less than the record first half of 1956.
Second, industrial production for June, 1957, was only slightly below the record level attained in October, 1956. It was not at the record level of October but I think all objective people would say that it was at a not unsatisfactory level.
Third, Canada's gross national product for the first and second quarters of 1957 substantially exceeded that of the same period of any earlier year, being estimated by the dominion bureau of statistics at $14.4 billion in contrast with $13.5 billion last year.
Fourth, labour income for June, 1957, reached an all-time high for any month of $1,327 million. More people had jobs than ever before and average weekly wages and salaries were likewise at an all-time high level.
Fifth, total retail trade for June, 1957, was greater than for any previous June, just as total retail trade for the first half of 1957 was substantially greater than for the first half of 1956.
Sixth, the total of gross domestic investment in housing, non-residential construction, machinery and equipment for the first half of 1957 constituted an all-time high for the first half of any year.
These few figures show quite clearly that when the present government assumed office toward the end of June this year Canada was enjoying a very high degree of prosperity and I suggest that this was the general conviction of Canadians at that time. But, Mr. Speaker, despite the prosperous state of affairs which existed last June, attention is now being focused upon the level of unemployment. The statistics for September, 1957, published jointly by the dominion bureau of statistics and the Department of Labour are disquieting and because they are disquieting I believe I should say something about this

The Address-Mr. Marler out to the government that nothing engenders fear and lack of confidence so much as does uncertainty; and it is a fair statement that the government is itself responsible for a great deal of the state of uncertainty which now prevails in Canada.
There is uncertainty as to the trade policies the government intends to follow. During the election campaign the Prime Minister repeatedly promised that he would call a conference of all commonwealth countries to discuss the problem of trade, so that Canada might recover the markets which he said the Liberals had lost. We know-but only in a very general way-of the efforts that have been made in connection with a commonwealth conference on trade, and we know that the government has organized a large mission of Canadians to visit the United Kingdom. But, Mr. Speaker, between the election campaign and the present time, a curious change has taken place.
The trade mission to the United Kingdom is proposing not to find out how the United Kingdom can be persuaded to buy more of our agricultural primary products and more of our manufactured goods but, on the contrary, its purpose is to try to persuade the British to sell to Canada more goods manufactured in the United Kingdom. In fact, we have been given the impression that it would be considered to be almost indecent for the trade mission to talk of the objectives which seemed so important during the election campaign. I say, Mr. Speaker, that this change of purpose is the kind of government action which promotes uncertainty in trade circles in Canada.
Then we also have the Prime Minister's offhand proposal to divert to the United Kingdom 15 per cent of the purchases Canadians make in the United States. There is uncertainty as to whether Canadians are to take this proposal in all seriousness, but this is of small moment compared to the uncertainty which the diversion of some $600 million of trade would have upon Canadian importers, distributors, retailers and consumers.
Then there is the uncertainty arising from the meetings at Mont Tremblant and at Ottawa of the representatives of the United Kingdom government and our own. What were the proposals put forward by the British, and what proposals were made by our own representatives? What are the policies being followed by our government? In response to a request for information the Minister of Finance made a statement which though spread over several pages of Hansard, gave no significant information whatever. Mr. Speaker, if I might just make a remark in parenthesis, it reminded me of the letter of a


school boy who feels that he must tell you what he did all day hour by hour from the time he woke up to the time he went to bed but who does not really tell you anything about what he was thinking or what he was going to do. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that even after listening to the statement of the Minister of Finance, both parliament and the nation itself are completely in the dark as to the trade policies the government intends to follow. We have more uncertainty.
Then there is uncertainty as to the policy to be followed by the government with respect to tight money. During the election campaign the Prime Minister repeatedly described for the benefit of Canadians the dire effects of the credit restrictions introduced by the Bank of Canada: they had struck a body-blow here and another body-blow there; small business had been strangled, and so on. Accordingly the electorate believed that the Conservative party was committed to putting an end to credit restrictions, and that belief was reinforced after the election by the statement made by the Minister of Finance as reported by the Ottawa Journal of June 26, 1957:
There very definitely must be early relaxation of the rigours of the tight money policy.
But, Mr. Speaker, despite repeated questions, hon. members have been unable to get from the government an answer as to what has been done to bring about such a relaxation; not what will be done but what has been done. The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Bell), in answer to such a question referred to "the many things that have been done" by the government. But no one on the government side of the house, Mr. Speaker, will provide one item of specific information on the subject. No one will say just what has been done.
The Minister of Finance on one or two occasions has alluded to the $150 million which the government has made available for housing; but surely no one will contend for an instant that the earmarking of that amount for housing has added to the available supply of money. All that has happened is that $150 million have been set aside for housing out of the total supply of money, and there is accordingly that much less available for other purposes. I am not complaining of this situation Mr. Speaker; I am merely drawing attention to the facts of the matter.
The Minister of Finance speaks of tight money as an unfortunate legacy from the Liberal government, and even the Prime Minister in his radio address last week blamed the Liberal government for the monetary policies which we followed. Mr. Speaker, if these statements are true, why

does not the present government-which has in the matter the same authority as had the previous government-implement its promises to the electors to change monetary policies; or, Mr. Speaker, if the statements are not well-founded, why does not the government admit the fact and tell parliament and the people of Canada what policy on credit restrictions they propose as an alternative? Surely in a matter such as this, and having regard to the conflict between the Conservatives' promises before the election and their silence and inactivity since that time, the people of Canada have a right to the kind of statement of government policy which will put an end to the uncertainties which the government has itself created.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance the other day referred to a slight reduction in the rate of interest now being paid by the Bank of Canada or by the government on treasury bills. He seemed to feel that this was a tremendous step forward. May I say that I have read with the closest interest and attention recently published statements of the Bank of Canada and their balance sheet, and I can see no indication whatever of any action taken by the Bank of Canada which has brought about this small reduction in the rate on treasury bills. I therefore ask myself, and I ask the government to tell us this: What has the government done to carry out its representations to the people of Canada that it would make a change in its policy with regard to tight money?
Then, Mr. Speaker, there is uncertainty as to the government's policies with respect to inflation. Before the election the Prime Minister was telling the country that federal government expenditures constitute the biggest inflationary factor in our economy, and that the Liberal government ought to cut its expenditures. Of course, that was before the election. What is the government's present policy?
We have very little to go on, Mr. Speaker, but though parliament has been in session only about a month, it has already authorized measures that will increase government expenditures by at least $200 million per annum, not counting either cash advances on farm stored grain amounting to another $100 or $150 million or the $150 million to be made available for housing, to which I referred a moment ago. In other words the government is going to have to find $500 million of new cash.
The contrast between the thousands of words of pre-election statements and the silence which the Prime Minister seems to have imposed upon his colleagues is indeed
The Address-Mr. Leboe surprising; just as the reduction of expenditures promised before the election contrasts strangely with the measures which the government has recommended to parliament.
We recall of course the promises of the Prime Minister to increase the payments to the provinces and also to reduce federal taxes, but how do all of these measures, whether adopted or contemplated, fit into the framework of a balanced budget? This is an important question, because the people of Canada I think should know at the earliest opportunity the budgetary policy to be followed by the present government. Nor is it unreasonable that the people of Canada should expect a statement from the government on this important subject. The policies advocated by the Prime Minister during the election were a change from those followed by the previous government and the people of Canada are entitled to know to what extent the promised change is to be carried out.
As I have endeavoured to point out, there is uncertainty as to the trade policies to be followed by the government; there is uncertainty as to its monetary policies; there is uncertainty as to its budgetary policies and there is even uncertainty as to whether it will present a budget during the current session.
I suggest that the government would be following a wise course if it sought to dispel these uncertainties by making clear, unequivocal statements of policy; by doing this they could remove many of the uncertainties with which Canadians are now faced and for which the government itself is fully responsible. It is an extraordinary thing, particularly having in mind the loquacity to which we became accustomed before the election, that so far no minister holding a portfolio in the government has participated in the present debate. May we expect some of them to do so before the debate concludes or is there to be uncertainty even on that point?
